- THE WOLF AT THE DOOR. "Do wolves go to poor people's doors, mamma? That is what the minister said When he came to ask for money to-day, And told you somebody's mother was dead." " Yes ! They do really, and stand and howl!" "Then it is dreadful to be poor. Just think how awful to go to bed When likely a wolt will be at the door! "With rich people too—are you sure, mamma? But then a policeman might drive them away; Rich people can have their houses watched, You know very well, all night and all day." " Another kind of wolf, but worse !" "Worse than the poor people's kind? Oh, say, Can it come to us? We are very rich; I heard a man say we were to-day." " Ah, darling, 'tis well you are afraid, The wolf is more frightful than you can guess? No ppliceman can drive him away. His terrible name is selfishness !" Mrs. M. F. Burrs.

NOTES ON VRICULTURE, HOR FT- CULTURE, &c.

• A new potato disease is reported from Norway. It is a vegetable fungus which rapidly reduces whole fields of pota- toes to the condition of withered straw. GIANT POTATO PLANT.—A farmer's wife of Milton Damerel planted a potato, giving it ample room. Now the stalk measures fully 19 inches around, and seven feet across the branches.— American. A gardener keeps his frames and hothouses free from slugs by mixing sulphate of copper with wheaten bread. The odour of the latter attracts the enemy to certain death. Keep poultry, however, from the stuff. Judith, 4 shorthorn heifer which carried the first prize at Aberdeen show on Thursday in the class for heifers in- milk, has been sold by Mr. Mitchell, of Auchnagathle, to Mr. Hewitt, for export to the United States. SHROPSHIRE SHEEP.—Mr. W. Cotterill, Derry, Ormond, has produced a Shropshire ram of very large dimensions on his farm and in his sheep-rearing sheds. The ram, which is only fifteen months old, is four feet long, two feet six inches high, one foot four and a half inches across the chest, I and three feet ten inches around the body. It is believed that Mr. Cotterill intends exhibiting the ram at Shrewsbury. THE LARGEST AGRICULTURAL MACHINE SHOP.— The most extensive agricultural, machine shops in the world are at Springfield, Ohio. There are five in all. A good idea of the immense size of one workshop may be obtained by ima- gining a building almost 17,000 feet in length by 60 feet in width, a continuous room three miles and over in length. At each minute a completely made machine is rolled from the stocks and housed or shipped to its destination; 600 machines from sunrise to sunset—an annual production of 100,000 implements.—Mechanical Engineer. The road heifer, Oxford Minstrel 4th, by Duke of Oxford 41st (38174), belonging to Mr. George Ashbumer, Low Hall, Kirkby Ireleth, has had her first calf, a heifer by Winsome Duke (45815). Mr. T. Allen, of Thurmaston Lodge, Leicestershire, has purchased from the Low Hall herd a young sire for use in his herd, viz., Baron Minstrel 3rd, a son of Mr. G. Ashburner's Baron Oxford 10th (42739) and Cambridge Minstrel. He is a dark roan, and was calved in April last. LETTING COWS TO LABOURERS.—A rather remarkable. feature has been Instituted by Mr. R. E. Turnbull, of Toyers Wood, near Hall. He lets out cows to labourers at a charge ,of about 25 per cent of their value, paid in advance. In seven years he has thus let out 150 cows, and the system is much to the advantage of the labourer, who gladly avails ; himself of it. Taking the hire at £5, and estimating the cost of keep at £l3 103. and the yield at £2B 10s., it will be seen that £lO is made as profit, in addition to the skim milk for the family. The advantage too of rearing a calf is con- siderable, for it enables the poor man to obtain a cow for himself at a minimum cost. SAVING PIG Mawunz.—The best way, says the National Lire Stock Journal, to save the entire liquid and solid drop- pings from pigs, is to make a slatted floor over a shallow manure vault. If a layer of muck is placed in the bottom of the vault, it will absorb all the liquid from the pigs, and this will prevent all bad odours. The pig is usually com- pelled to lie in his own filth, and this has given him a bad name. These slats are placed one inch apart, and the liquid runs through into the vault, and the solid manure is trodden through, and the result is that all the manure is saved, and that the pigs are kept clean. The food is given in troughs, and not on the floor. A ROYAL SHOW BEAST SLAUGHTERED.—Mr. Bartlemore's celebrated Ayrshire bull, Baron o' Bucklyvie was, after his victory at the Royal English show, sent to the butcher, be- cause of a viciousness of temper rendering him dangerous to work with. This was the best Ayrshire bull that has been seen in the showyard of recent years, and he has left some good prize-taking animals behind him. The Baron won for his late owner during the three last seasons, 30 gold and silver medals and 6 valuable cups, besides 25 first prizes in money, and twice in succession the Ayrshire Cattle Herd- Book Society's special premium at Ayr, as the best Herd- _ _

No bank should be without a chest protector. How to get out of a scrape—Let your beard grow. An unhappy marriage is like an electric machine; it makes one dance, but you can't let go. When you think the world cannot get along without you, pull a hair from your head and see if it makes you bald- headed. The sight of a fat man trying to look graceful in a bath- ing suit is what makes the little baldheaded fishes stind on their tails and grin. If you would live in an atmosphere of benevolence, make it your study to be always rendering others service, and never hesitate to ask the same of them. All women can talk with their eyes. The tongue is there- fore a useless appendage to the sex ; still there are women who have found something for it to do. A girl was recently arrested, being disguised as an old woman. if all the old women who appear in the disguise of girls were arrested, the gaols would have the appearance of sardine boxes. Would you be at peace with your conscience? Let God find you at each moment of the day doing one of these four things, which once formed the rule of a saintly life :—(1) Praying, (2) labouring, (3) striving after holiness, (4) prac- tising patience. Would you become holy? Try to add to the above Actions the following virtnes:—Method, faith, spiritual combat, perseverance. A man being examined in an important case, counsel found it extremely difficult to extract the whole truth from him; his ingenuity and ignorance combined enabled him to evade the questions. At last the lawyer, losing patience, exclaimed, 6' Why, sir, do you prevaricate so much?" The witness, supposing he referred to his peculiar manner of utterance, convulsed the Court and audience by replying indignantly, "I would like to know how a fellow can help prevaricating when he has lost three of his frimt teeth?' A friend tells us of a dinner scene which happened at Airth in the last generation. Mrs. Murray, of Abercairney, had been amongst the guests, and at dinner one of the family noticed that she was looking for the proper spoon to help herself with salt. The old servant, Thomas, was ap- pealed to that the want might be supplied. He did not notice the appeal. It was repeated in a more peremptory manner—" Thomas, Mrs. Murray has not a salt-spoon." To which he replied, most emphatically, "Last time Mrs. Murray dined here we lost a salt-spoon." At the sale of an antiquarian gentleman's effects in Rox- burghshire, which Sir Walter Scott happened to attend, there was one little article, a Roman patina, which occa- sioned a good deal of competition, and was eventually knocked down to the distinguished baronet at a high price. Sir Walter was excessively amused, during the time of bid- ding, to observe how much it excited the astonishment of an old woman, who had evidently come there to buy culin- ary utensils on a more economical principle. "If the par- ritch-pan," she at last burst out, "if the parritch-pan gangs at that, what will the kail-pat gang for?" Near a fruit stand a little shaver noticed a dime lying upon the ground, which had doubtless been dropped by the owner, a big-handed countryman. He picked up the coin and handed it to the man, who, pleased with the boy's honesty, said, "That is nice in you. Always be honest and you will get along. An I here, help yourself to a handful of cherries." "Thank you, sir ; but I would rather that you should give them to me." "Never mind; help your- self. Don't be bashful," said the farmer." "That isn't the trouble exactly, sir," answered the boy; "but you see, your hand is bigger than mine." A double hand, heaping full, was laughingly given him by the farmer. THE INDIAN JESTEIL AND THE THlEVES.—Tenndram was a famous buffoon of the Court of a great Prince in the East. One evening, whilst conversing with his wife in the parlour, he found out that thieves were lurking about the house. He told his wife in a loud voice, "My dear, I am afraid that thieves are prowling in the neighbourhood ; it is better we put all our wealth in our great wooden box and drop it into our garden well." So saying, he filled a box with heavy atones and rubbish, and, securing it with locks, dropped it into the well. The thieves, imagining that Tennelram had given them a very fair opportunity of walking away with his riches, began to drain the well, with the object of taking out the box. Tennellem, in the dark, set in order the garden channels, which had long been neglected, and the water flowed into the beis. The night had far advanced, and yet no box appeared, as the well was very deep ; and when the dawn broke out the thieves gave up the hopeless task and slowly crept out of the garden. Tennelrarn, who had just then finished the very agreeable task of irrigating his gar- den, exclaimed, "I am very thankful to you for having taken the trouble of watering my garden! Should you feel inclined, you may come some other day and drain the well and take the box, for I assure you it will remain where you have left it at present."—Leisure Hour. SHIPPING FOR HEALTH AND BEAUTY.—An old-fashioned, graceful, yet much-neglected form of amusement for chil- dren is the use of the skipping-rope. It is one of the healthiest exercises ever invented, and it probably dates from prehistoric times. Boys, unless they are very little, consider it exclusively a girlish pastime, but the exercise is just as good for them as for their sisters. Skipping back- wards instead of forwards should always be encouraged, as it throws open the chest and developes the muscles of the arms and shoulders. The girl who skips much and well is sure to be lithe, supple, and light in her movements, while the exereisels good in every way for her bodily health. It is, however, hardly an amusement for very hot weather, but rather for the cold, fine, bracing days of spring and autumn, or, if there be plenty of room to play indoors, for wet or snowy wintry days when there is no getting out. A learned lady, the widow of a French savant who retained perfect health to extreme old age, and whose dainty figure was as round and slender at seventy as it had been at seventeen, always declared that the secret of her juvenility was her skipping-rope. Every day she skipped for half an hour, out of doors if possible, or in the hall if it were sufficiently capacious. When visiting friends she usually skipped in the retirement of her own bedroom, but she would never have packed her trunks without putting in her skipping- rope, even if she had left her best bonnet behind to make room for it. I must not, however, malign her, for she rarely wore the machine called a bonnet when her youth and mid- dle age were past, but had. a comfortable black silk hood which protected her ears' face, and neck, and being lined with delicate blue or pink, and put on over a cap of costly lace, was very becoming. When she died she left her skipping-rope and a pair of battledores and shuttlecocks as a legacy to a little maid who was her faraway kinswoman, saying that they had been among her best friends and had accompanied her all over Europe. Coms•roN.—Two roads conduct from Ambleside to Conis- ton. It is better to take the more southern course in going aud the other in returning. At first the scenery is rich and park-like ; then, as the road ascends, it becomes somewhat wilder. Windermere lies below and behind; the sheet of liquid blue, which rivals the sky, widening out as you mount. The crags of Langdale and Oxenfell stand boldly out; these on the day that I passed, were bathed in a light more like that of Italy than of England. Crags and glassy slopes, green fields and heather-clad moors, firs, juniper, and a hundred other shrubs, gave each moment new combinations, changing, as in a kaleidoscope, from beauty to beauty, till the blue sheet of Coniston opened out before us, its head em- bosomed in trees. and guarded by the massive form of the far-famed Old Man. The view from the summit of this mountain, in my opinion, is one of the finest in the district. Standing as it were upon a bastion tower on the edge of the group, we command a wide extent of the higher mountains, the bolder peaks of Scawfell range along the beautiful lake, "eniineY almost under our feet, and thence far down the estuary of the Kent, the Leven, and the Duddon, to the sands of Morecambe Bay. Far away over these may be seen on a clear die,' the castle of Lancaster, and even Ingle- borough .and the Yorkshire fells; while those who are specially favoured may discern, like clouds on the horizon, the Isle of Man, and even the peak of Snowdon. The Old Man, like most of the -Caseeheiani mountains, is easily ascended, a good path leading up to the rounded platform which forms the top ; and the pedestrian who is impatient of this can readily climb the steep alePeeee of the central corrie. A friend of mine, however, once met with a novel adventure on his descent along the northern ridge of the mountain, for he was attacked by a golden eagle, which dashed down at him again and again with great fury. As he had no better weapon of defence than an umberella, the bird had an unfair advantage or the biped. Its mode of attack was to circle -above him at some distance, and then suddenly,swooPdown "all claws upon the foe." As in one of these attacks it actually got within his guard, he was not sorry when, after some quarter of an hour of warfare, it at last desisted and sailed majestically back to its eyrie. From some points of view the trench-like form of Coniston Lake Is a little too conspicuous for perfect beauty, but it would be difficult to And anywhere more lovely views than are obtained from several places near the upper end. Sweeps of greenest grass, and groves of trees of many shades, from the dark fir to the bright lime, make exquisite foregrounds for the blue expanse of water and the massive form of the Old Man. In one of the most beautiful of these sights is the house of Profeeebt Ruskin' to whom, as so many other poets, the spell of Cumbrian beauty has proved an irrestible attraction. The lover of the picturesque cannot help lingering in view of She home of one who, more than any other man, has taught his countrymen to appreciate the greatest master of landscape-pa!nting the world has ever produced, and has zealously striven to convert students of Nature from follow- ing false ideals to seeking- for her truths and reverencing her beauty.—" Picturesque Europe."

Book bull in the Yard. TRICHIN/E.—J. E. Morris, M.D., in the Clinical Brief, says, in regard to trichina 3 in swine, that it is a well- established fact that the real source of infection in swine lies entirely in the rat. A committee of Vienna physicians found in Moravia 37 per cent. of rats examined trichinous, in Vienna and its environs 10 per cent., and in Lower Aus- tria 4 per cent. The well-known voracity of the hog, and its special fondness for meat, cause it to feed upon the flesh and excrements of- other animals infested with these para- sites, and especially rats and mice. To prevent trichinous swine, it is highly important to cut off all the sources of disease in the diet of these animals. SINGULAR Mrsuar.—Whilst a geoom in the employ of Mr. W. R. Brown was engaged in " lungeing " a valuable horse belonging to that gentleman on his estate at Highfield on Thursday last, the rope broke, and the animal finding itself free, at once galloped furiously down the field. The unfortunate creature, however, was soon arrested in its mad career, for it stepped on the rein that was dangling from its head, and stumbling, fell with terrific force head fore- most against the trunk of a tree, killing itself instantly Somewhat strange to relate, its neck was not broken, nor was there scarcely any abrasion of the skin on the animal's forehead. It was valued at 200 guineas. A BURIED SOW.—According to a Toronto paper, a re- markable instance of tenacity of life on the part of a sow, occurred quite recently. It seems the animal had disap- peared for nearly two months and a half, and her owner, after making many a seareh for her, at. Lust concluded that she had been devoured by wolves. A neighbour having oc- casion to remove some straw from a stack, had taken away several loads, when he heard noises, proceeding, as he im- agined, from a pig. More straw having been removed, he was fortunate enough to discover the missing sow. Instead of a living skeleton, she presented the appearance of health and liveliness. She had subsisted on nothing but straw for ten weeks.—Little Folks. CLEANLINESS IN THE DAIRY.—The best butter comes from the most intelligent and observing operators. Stu- pidity never makes good butter. Intelligence is always al valuable constituent in the qualifications and "make up" , of the operatives in any industry, but it is indispenable in the fine art of butter making. Innocent consumers are often made the victims of filthy and unwholesome praetices, ply beca Ise the operatives in the dairy have not intelligence enough to distinguish between what is and what is not filthy and detrimental, or, if they have the ability, they neglect to use-it. Thus dairymen frequently do unwillingly what they would scorn and most sedulously avoid if they had a clear appreciation of the consequences their conduct involves.— National Live-Stock Journal, Chicago. NEW VARIETY OF WHEAT.—In growing new varieties of wheat, the tendency of the English and Americans has been to secure such as are very productive, giving a fine white flour. Braune, in Biendorf, has undertaken to pro- duce wheat which would combine with these advantages an earlier ripening, and has succeeded, by crossing productive winter and summer wheat, in -growing the German July wheat. This matures about three weeks earlier than the English varieties, and is said not to be inferior to the latter, either in productiveness or in the whiteness of the flour. The July wheat is not bearded, and, like all unbearded varieties, gives a finer flour and less bran than the bearded. The new wheat was raised on marshy as well as on sandy soil, with equally good results. In the fertilisers used, phosphoric acid was predominant. The height of the wheat is from 120 to 125 cm., and its ears are from 12 to 16 cm. in length. The wheat matures about the end of July, and does not fall within the period of severe rains, which generally occur in August. The berry of the wheat is of a medium size. Its colour is reddish, and its lustre is in no way inferior to that of Grecian summer wheat.—Oest. Ung. Muller. THE PRINTER'S DEVIL -X. [BY ANGLO-SCOTUS.] (The riyht of re-publication is reserved.) I alluded in paper No. VII. to the Hen and Chicken disaster. Well, some of the German news- papers made fun at gip sentence of the court-martial en the officers of that ship. "How can you," asked tho editor of one Teutonic paper, " dismiss a in tri front a ship that lies at the bettotn of the ocean? " The i came editor the next week publiehed sit account of the trial at Munich of a sergeant who had attacked a civilian with his sabre, and severely wounded him. The prisoner was :teemed of maliciously cutting and wounding, and the evidence against him was conclusive; but the court actually acquitted him on the ground that 'a sword does not partake of the nature of a lethal weapon." This was hoisting one's-self by means of a home-made petard with a vengeance! The fol- lowing extract from Egyptian General Orders may be con- siderate, but it is hardly comforting :—" 0. C. regiments and corps arc informed that coffins can be procured at the Royal Engineers' Stores at Abbassiyeh and Citadel. The contract price is 245. each." Dean Alford relates that the following lucid notice to engine drivers was exhibited at an English railway station :—" Hereafter, when trains moeing in an opposite direction are approaching each other on separate lines, conductors and engineers will be required to bring their respective trains to a dead halt before the point of meeting, and be very careful not to proceed till each train has passed the other." That is almost as good as the vagary of the compositor who made the Quaker friend of Wordsworth "travel on a pony from Yarmouth to London, to attend the yearly meeting of the Fiends." Of course 't Friends " was meant. And "the scene of some celebrated event clambering over the ruins of hoary castle or abbey to hear the aisles of one of our lively cathedrals," would indeed be a sight to see. Talk about earthquakes after this! The address of a certain Dr. 1 Lomas to Dr. Holmes contained the following side-split- ting notice :—" I pledge you in the name of my comrades and brothers, that the kindly regard that we now offer you shall live from the pleasant hour we slow enjoy together to that far distant one when you shall leave us, to occupy your predestined niche in the Walhalla of fame surrounded as with a garment by that glory which kills the sepulchre, and embalms a man that he 111,07 live among the immortal ones that were not born to die.'; As the reviewer who drew attention to the blunder remarked, "If Dr. Holmes kept a straight face while he was being thus embalmed among the immortal ones that were not born to die,' he came suc- cesefully through the severest test to which his gratitude could be put." Of course the two italicised words should have been respectively "name " and " it." In the" Miscellaneous Essays" ef the late W. R. Greg, the printers make Misa Harriet Martineau speak of "Christians clinging to their man-dog," instead of "man-god." And the comp. who made an assemblage of persons "waggle their hands," instead of their heads, must have had =dolls ideas about human anatomy. The following is not a bed exame le of the " bold, imaginative style" :—" The Stan- dard Oil Works in Jersey city were set on fire on-- by lightning. Tank after tank exploded! The flames were seen twenty-four miles off ! ! Ponderous pieces of tank were thrown a distance of half a mile! ! ! The crowds who as- sembled on the top of a neighbouring hill a mile away were scorched! !! ! " This is how a certain individual trans- lated two lines of the " : " Autolveus held up the meat. Divine tysscs sliced it." But all the 7,405,927 devils must have joined forces and guided the fingers of the American Johnson who wrote the so-called Indian love-song in which the following lines occur And to beguile the NT, yage, if thou wilt come aboard. Till sunset fire the waters, the fire-water shall be peered." Only the Printer's Devil, aided by the 7,405,9'26 satellites, could suggest that a couple of lovers should, in order the better to make love to one another, get boezey on the buoy- ant water. And who but the Devil could put it into a man's mind to make the following assertion "A thousand thongs flora thy dear hide are knotted round my avid." The thongs ought to be doubly knotted and switched with a vigorous arm about a more solid part of that poet's ana- tomy. But the refrain to the song in question-bangs all. Here it is "Then clad in noiseless mecaelins the feet of the year shall •fall, For I will cherish thee, my love, till time shall scalp us all." This man ought to be "solaced" in the ancient Caxtonian manner, with the "ten pounds and a purse," by the strongest man in the chapel. They would skelp him, without waiting till old Father Time came along, with or without his mo- assine.

IN AN ENGLISH BT-WAY.—In the first field I lighted upon a charcoal-burner plying his craft, and being curious to see how he went to work, pulled up besides his little hut and gave him greeting. At first he seemed astonished at being addressed; but presently, actuated apparently. by a sudden determination to equal the stranger in civility, he came up to me, and, without any kind of warning, poked me familiarly in the side with his grimy fist, and asked me with a chuckle what I thought about Egypt,now. I may presume that the coat which I wore upon this occasion was of a light gray, and the impression which the charcoal- burner made upon me, or rather upon my coat, was not, , therefore, altogether favourable. " bo'ee think it'll be a war ?" he inquired, grinning all over his cot-black face. I replied ina—l-cleusly that at the present stage of affairs it was impossible to say. "They'll do it if they has to go into it, doin't 'ee think so?, continued my sable friend, leaving an. other impression of his fist upon my garment, and laughing with an infinite enjoyment of the political situation. "A young man says to me last night, Alexandra's all very well, but they want teake the next pleace."Woiint they?' says I. 'You beiint old enough to remember Alma," he added, measuring me from top to toe, as if he would esti- mate my age by my height; "but they took that, didn't 'em ?--went right up i' feace o' the guns l'?Ancl-at this climax he went off into an uncontrollable fit of laughter till his sides shook again with merriment, and ended by 'piling. ing his bare black elbow into my ribs in a confidential man- ner, as 'though this piece of history were a private jest be- tween him and me. Out of consideration for my person2a appearance, I thought it better to discontinue this conver- sation, so bade the charcoal-burner "Good morning," aild left him to his work.—" Down the Rotlter," lj Herbert Rix, in Good Words, for August.

A VISIT TO PARIS VIA LONDON AND BRIGHTON. First I most mention, in speaking of Paris, the ex- ternal splendour of the city, which makes our English cities look dirty and dismal in comparison' and after- wards speak of the internal magnificence. The delight- ful boulevards with avenues of trees on each side first attracted attention, and caused us to think that even cities could be made pleasant to live in. Many of the boulevards are very long, very wide, and very handsome. We liked particularly that running into the city through the Arc de Triomphe, the Place de la Concorde, and the Garden of the Tuileries. It is known for the greater part of its length as the Champs Elyse6s, and the beautiful grounds here with their monuments, fountains, gardens, and groves all on the level, are well worthy of a title meaning Elysian fields. It was so pleasant to be driven about in waggonettes on the asphalte roads of the boulevards that I must make a remark upon it, and mention the reason why asphalte is used instead of a stone pavement. During the revolutions and insur- rections the stones were'so frequently pulled up and used to form barricades, thtt in 1850 a large portion of the present asphalte roadway was laid down. Among the buildings that we visited, or passed, were some fine specimens of the Corinthian order of architecture, in- cluding tht. Church of the Madeleine, and the Bourse ,(or Exchang,.). In St. Chapelle we saw "an architectural gem," the most beautiful Gothic edifice in Paris; and in the Louvre, whose galleries contain about the largest and finest collection of works of art in the world, we had at our very doors a magnificent palace, which is considered to be a very fine specimen of French Renaissance. The Trocadero, a charmingly-designed building, where the Exhibition of 1878 was held, attracted much admiration, and so did the Opera House, and many other imposing edifices of more or less architectural pretensions. Special attention was directed to the beautiful towers of the Notre Dame, as compared with the dissimilar and unsymetrical ones of the neigh- bouring church, St. Sulpice, and we were told that when St. Sulpice was in course of erection, a mandate was in force that no two towers of any church, save Notre Dame itself, should be of equal design and height. Our travels, covering over 1000 miles of land and water, were more enjoyable than we could reasonably hope for. The channel crossing, and the railway excursion through Normandy from Diem:l(ft° Paris, were the most enjoyable bits. Fortunately the channel was smooth both on going and returning, and, though travelling by the night boats, it was broad daylight when we arrived at Dieppe going, and the same when we arrived at Newhaven on the return passage, which gave us an opportunity of admiring the white chalk cliffs of the coast-line on both sides. The boats were de- ficient in sleeping accommodation and we had expense as well as difficulty in securing berths. Each way the passage occupied about six and a half hours, but on the outward journey we had eleven hours on board, as we had four and a half hours to wait for the tide after embarking. The railway journey through Normandy, being chiefly along the course of the Seine, was very pleasant. We had the opportunity of breaking our journey at Rouen," the Manchester of France," but did not avail ourselves of it. Another privilege accorded we did take advantage of, namely, travelling round by Brighton, and breaking the journey both there and in London.

Brighton, so well known to Lancashire men and women because we have a seaside resort very often compared to it, is a charming watering place on the south coast of England, where the wealthy citizens of the world's metropolis spend a good deal of their time, having excellent- express railway connection enabling them to attend to their daily business without inconvenience. Blackpool is often called "The Brighton of the North," and the best description that can be given of Brighton is that it is something like Blackpool. We had a drive along the whole length of its promenade, which did not appear to be so well kept as that at Black- pool, and we also drove through some of the principal squares and crescents which make its architectural sea frontage much superior to the frontage at Blackpool. There are two piers, as at Blackpool, one an old chain pier, and the other somewhat similar to the North Pier at Blackpool. 1 We were highly delighted with our short excursion to Brighton, though we should certainly not go all the way from Blackburn specially to visit it. The view seaward was very interesting, there being many ocean-going vessels at full sail in the Channel.

In London we spent one whole day in sight seeing, and more in loitering about. As we had all visited London before, we skipped the usual sights, with the exception of Westminster Abbey and St. Paul's Cathedral—both of which are superior to anything of the kind in Paris—and devoted the greater portion of our sight-seeing day to the International Fisheries Exhibition. There we saw illustrations of modes of sea fishirg in all parts of the world, and real fishing boats of every descrip- tion, from the light coracle of the ancient Briton and the modern Celt, to the most improved build of powerful whale boats fitted with musket-harpoons and other ingenious con- trivances. The life-saving apparatus, including one im- mense life-boat 'end many smaller ones, was a study in itself. The very boat in which Grace Darling so heroically dis- tinguished herself was a centre of attraction. We glided quickly through the departments representing many foreign countries, merely stopping to compare or contrast their fishing tackle with our own. The Aquarium we only casually inspected, and from the voluminous appearance of the official catalogue we concluded that we did not even put our eyes on the hundreth part of the exhibits collected in the buildings. This was before going to Paris. Our list days in London, on the return journey, Were variously spent. The weather, which we had had hot and fine in France, Was cold and wet in England, and this had some- thing to do with our arrangements. For my own part I was content to "rest and reflect," and to ratnble leisurely on Richmond Hill, where I was staying, or along the banks of Old Father Thames. The rambling, however, was only during the half hours of the sunshine that fortune smiled upon us.

We arrived safely home, at various times, one on the eighth, another on the ninth, and a third ox the four- teenth day after departure. Our tickets were each avail- ab!e for sixteen days, but our leave of absence had not the same uniformity. J. G. S.
A rich widow is the only second-hand article that brings

a first-class price. There are some marriages which remind us of the poor fellow who said, "She couldn't get any huaband, and I couldn't get any wife, so we got married." ; Nellie was visiting Niagara Falls with her father. See- ing the foam at the foot of the great cataract, she ex- claimed, "Papa, how much soap it must take to make so much suds !"

An American piper says :—New York pays 7,000,000 dole. a year for its religion and 22,000,000 dols. for its drinks, which goes to show that New York is hiving more fun in this world than it will in tho neat.

"What is the difference between the youths' and the men's departments at the big clothing shop ?" asked an Irish- man of a friend; and receiving no reply, he continued: "Because at the wan I buys me ..clothes, and at the other I clothes me b'ys."

I "When I grow up I'll be a man, won't I?" asked a little boy of his mother. "Yes, my son; but if you want to be a man, you must be industrious at school, and learn how to behave yourself." "Why, mamma, are lazy boys women when they grow up." A formal fashionable visitor thus addressed a little girl: How are you, my dear ?" "Very well, I thank you,' she replied. The visitor then added: "Now, my dear, ytu should ask me how I am." The child simply and honestly replied: "But I don't:want to know." THE BIG PUBIPHIN SEASON.—The San Francisco Post says: —A Los Angelos rancher has raised a pumpkin so large that his two children use a half each for a cradle. This may seem very wonclarjul in the rural districts, but in , this city three or four full-grown policemen have been found asleep on a single beat, I "I only want to show you one thing more, Professor. I have invented a abort method of boring mountains, which I think will 'prove very valuable." "My dear sir," burst forth the, *wearied listener, "if you would only invent a slort method of boring individuals, you would indeed con- fer a lasting benefit on the human race." EXPLOSION OF GUN COTTON: ONE MAN KILLED AND THREE INJURED.—An explosion of gun cotton occurred on Thursday morning, at the new James Watt Dock, Greenock. A niece of rock weighing fifteen tons was blown forty yards, and fell on a labourer, named Cungstie killing him in- stantly. Another man named Angus Mleod was thrown twenty-five feet, and so terribly injured he is not expected to survive. Two others were hurt, but not seriously. IMPORTANT DECISION UNDER THE EMPLOYERS'-LIABIL- ITY Ac—The Judge of the Hanley County Court (Mr. T. H. Jordan) has had before him a case of some importance , under the Employers' Liability Act. The plaintiff, a collier, I sued in respect of injuries caused by a fall of roof. The mishap arose from defective propping— the work of another collier—and the plaintiff admitted that he knew that the , roof timbers were defective, but that he made no complaint until after the accident. There was no proof in the Judge's opinion of negligence on the part of any person entrusted , by the defendant to see to the safety of the mine; but his , Honour held, mreover, that by the termlof the Act an in- - jured workman could not recover if he knew of the danger and did not complain of it within a reasonable time. , A COMPARATIVE TRIFLE.—The Kentuckian admiration for fine horses is the strongest feeling in his nature. He , cares very little whether or not the public entertains a favourable opinion of him, but he wants everyone to think well of his horse. Some time ago the editor of the Ken- tucky State Journal, published at Newport, Ky., published a local item concerning a horse well known in the community. Shortly afterwards a man entered the office with a revenge- , ful air and said: "My name'is Squire Jaggles, and lam not a tender-hearted man, let me tell you. I understand that you have flung reflections on the character of my horse." "I don't know," replied the other, "that I said anything derogatory to the character of your horse. I merely in- sinuated that you stole the animal, but I did not say any- thing to in the least injure his character." "That's all right, then; I don't care who says I stole him, but blamed if any man shall say that he can't run." THE SNARE-GOD OF DAHOMEY.—The most powerful fetish is Danh-gbwe, the tutelary saint of Whydah, which is personified by the harmless snake so named. Its worship was introduced into Dahomey when the kingdom of Whydah was conquered and annexed. In Whydah, hidden from eyes profane by a thick grove of fig-trees, is the famed Danh-hweh, or fetish snake-house. It is, according to Mr. Skertchy, nothing more than a circular swish hut—the very model of the Parian inkstand to be seen in every toy-shop. From the room depended pieces of cotton yarn, and on the floor, which, in common wi;h the walls, was whitewashed, were several pots of water. The pythons, to the number of twenty-two, were coiled on the top of the wall or twined around the rafters. All those hideous reptiles are sacred. To slay one, even by accident—for to do so purposely would not be dreamt of—used to entail instant sacrifice to the gods, and confiscation of all the offender's property to the fetish priests. Nowadays his punishment is not so severe, but still exemplary enough. The offender, after a meeting of all the fetishers of the neighbourhood is convened, is seated within a hut of stick, thached with dry grass and built in the enclosure in front of the snake-house. His clothes and body are well daubed with palm-oil, mixed with the fat of the murdered snake-god. At a given signal the hut is fired, and the materials being like tinder, the unfortunate offender against the majesty of the fetish is enveloped in flames. In excruciating torture he rushes out of the flames—his clothes on fire—to the nearest water, pursued by the infurated priests, who belabour him with sticks, stones, and all sorts of rub- bish. If he reaches the water he is free, and if he is fortu- nate to live, has expiated his crime. But few are able to run the gannlet, and expire before reaching the cooling water, clubbed to death by the fetishmen—theDan-gblee-no, or snake-mothers, as they are called. As the door of the snake-temple is always open, the snakes frequently wander out after nightfall. If any person meets one, he must prostrate himself before it, carrying it tenderly in his arms to the temple when his humanity to the snake-god is rewarded by his being fined for meeting the snake ; and ki he cannot or will not pay, is imprisoned until the uttermosi cowry is extracted from him.—" The -,People of the World.''

div.head: AIISCELLANEOITS
div.p: AIISCELLANEOITS

The anneal report of the Amalgamated Society of Rail- way Servants, just issued, shows that the funds increased during the year by nearly £5.000. Captain H. F. Monteith, governor of Her Majesty's General Prison, Perth, died on Tuesday morning after a Prolongel illness. Captain Monteith, who was 42 years of • age, was appointed governor of Perth Prison in August last. A COSTLY SNORE—On Saturday, at Derby, a publican, named Upton, was charged by the Midland Railway Com- Pally with annoying passengers by smoking in a non- smoking compartment, and refusing to desist when requested to .do so. The fine and costs amounted to £6 ss. 6d. The licensing dispute having disappeared, Lord Zetland is again ingratiating himself with the people of Grange- mouth. Provost Macpherson has received a letter from the Earl' e commissioners, intimating that his lordship intends subscribing £5OO towards the erection of a proposed new town hall. On Sunday afternoon, whilst a mason, named Hargreaves, was employed in a new main sewer at Accrington, a fall of earth buried him up to the neck. Rain began to descend, and ',as water slowly accumulated in the excavation, he unfortunate man,who could not be freed, was drowned in spite of efforts to pump out the water by fire engines. Two tourists have lost their lives on the Grampians. The death is reported of the Rev. G. S. Kelly, of Dundee, while endeevouring to go from Braemar over Lochnagar to Ballater ; and on Sunday William Morrison, a carpenter from Aberdeen, who with a companion, had scaled Loch- agar, fell down a cliff about a thousand feet high, and was instantly killed. Camp MURDER AND ATTEMPTED SUICIDE. Susan Matilda Ludlow, wife of a joiner living at Holloway, who has been in a desponding condition for some time, drowned OH Se turday, in a cistern outside her residence, her little girl, two years old. Before the deed was discovered the woman lied, and was arrested at Canonbury when attempting to commit suicide •in the New River. There appears to be Re doubt that she is insane. THROWING BOILING WATER ON A WIFE.—A woman • namei Marie Rudge is now lying at Bolton Irfirmary suf- fering from injuries w ich she states were inflicted by her husband in a locleing-house in King-street. On Saturday ' night both were the worse for liquor, and Rudge, during a quarrel, seized a kettle of boiling water standing on the fire and poured it over her. She was removed to the In- firmary, where her depositions were taken. Rudge has dis- appeared. A SURGEON'S CERTIFICATE NOT LIBELLOUS.—At Bow- street, on Saturday, Mrs. Weldon applied for a summons against Dr. Forbes Winslow upon an allegation that he had libelled her by stating that she was insane. Mr. Flowers refused to grant the summons, stating that there was no reason for believing that Dr. Winslow had acted in any Other way than in the exercise of his profession by signing a Certificate, and that that could not be considered libellous. The Earl of Dalhousie, in-the course of a speech at a Liberal meeting at Bow on Monday, remarked that the suc- cess; of the Government hal been in the degree it had de- Parted from the policy of its predecessor. He was full of hope as to the future, but the mintier, cared for many things Which members of the House of 'Commons were not in earnest about, and there would have to be a reform of Par- liament and a redistribution of seats before any large or Solid measures were passed into law. A CLERGYMAN IN Taornen.—The Rev. George William Elliott, whose friends reside at Wolverhampton, was on Tuesday brought up under the Vagrancy Act at Salisbury. He was found under a rick in a village without any visible • means of subsistence. His letters of orders were found on him. He had been four times curate of a parish. His friends Were communicated with, but they refused to help him. The bench, taking into c msideration the fact that the reverend gentleman had been in custody several days, dis- charged him. A. ROYAL CONCERT.—The Duchess of Connaught and Princess Christian took part on Seturday at a concert given at Ascot in aid of the fund for the completion of St. Anne's Church, 13agshot, the erection of which is mainly attribu- table to the exertions of the Duke of Connaught and the Parishioners of the pleasant little Surrey village adjoining hi a Royal Highness's demesne. In the course of the con- cert Princess Christian and Mr. Parrett played a pianoforte selection, by Chopin and Saint-Saens. The Duchess of Connaught made her first essay in public as a vocalist. Her Royal Highness sang "The last dream," by Bowen, and a cbansonet, by Alary. MYSTERIOUS DISAPPEARANCE OF A CLERGYMAN.—Much _apprehension has been excited among the friends of the nein Merton Smith, vicar of Plymton, Devon, at the dis- appearance of that gentleman under circumstance.; creating; the !gayest anxiety. He left England ten days ago, accom- panied by his brother-in-law. the Rev. J. Murray, rector of Rugby for a tour in the Pyrenees. Last Wednesday, after breakfast, Mr. Smith left the hotel where they were staying for a stroll alone, and nothing has been heard of him since. It is supposed that the missing gentleman, who was in ex- cellent health and spirits, has either been captured by brigands or fallen down a precipice. NATIONAL RADICAL FEDERATION.—A meeting, convened bY the National Radic il Federation, was held in the Vic- toria Chambers, Westminster,' on Monday, for the purpose of considering how best to improve and extend Radical organisations throughout the country. In the course of the Proceedings a letter was read from Mr. Gladstone conveying his thanks for the expression of approval and confidence in the Government contained in a resolution passed at a pro- Ylous meeting of the federation. It was resolved to take immediate steps to form bran Ches of the federation, and to unite the Radical cause in Liverpool, Sheffield, Manchester, Leeds, Bristol, and other large provincial centres. A MUSIC HALL BURNED DOWN: NARROW ESCAPE OF THE AUDIENCE.—About half-past seven on Saturday even- ing, a fire broke out at Durland's Star Music Hall, Upper Sans-street, Sunderland, and resulted in the destruction of the building. The flames were perceived near the roof above the stage, when Constable Sanderson and Mr. Dur- lane, eroprietor, adopted promnt measures to get out the audience, numb:ring from 1,000 to 1,300. Their efforts were successful in averting a panic, and in four minutes the ball was clear without personal mishap. Engines were Speedily at work, but at eight o'clock the roof fell in, and the building was soon in ruins. The fire was extinguished by nine o'clock, thoueh water was still being thrown upon the embers up to a late hour. THREE BROTHERS DROWNED IN THE THAMES.—A plea- Sure boat accident, resulting in the drowning of three men, occurred near Battersea Bridge, Chelsea, on Saturday night. It appears that three brothers engaged a boat at Green's boat-house, Chelsea, about half-past five o'clock. After rowing across the river, and when off Wakeley's Wharf, one of the men stood up in the boat, which immediatety capsized, and the whole of the occupants were drowned. Five boats immediately put off with drags, but they failed to recover the bodies. At sewn o'clock the Thames police arrived at the scene of the disaster, and soon succeeded in dragging up two bodies. The two brothers were clasped in one another's arms. One of them was an ex-soldier, and the other a wheelwright. The third brother was found by a water- Man. THE NATIONAL DERT.—Two Parliamentary returns issued ea Tuesday give the latest figures of the National Debt. One sets forth the particulars of the debt as at the 31st Of March. 1883, the net value of the debt on that day being £723,768,087 4s. 6d. The terminable annuties, which are stated in detail, show an annual charge of £7X0,984 us. Id., their capital value being £27,570,876. The other return shows the operation of the Commissioners for the reduction of the National Debt, arranging the various sums received from the Exchequer under specified heads, inclu- ding terminable annuities, old and new sinking funds, and the particular application of them in the year ending March 31, 1883. The total of the Exchequer issue representing repayment of capital in reduction of debt was £7,149,284 15s. 7d. Selby, Miss J. King, Miss K. Forrest, Miss M. Thomas, Miss A. Crisp, Miss A Yardley, Miss A. K. Holland, Mrs. Janet King, Miss Hornor. Mn. GLADSTONE AND HIS CONSTITUENTS. It is con- sidered certain in Midlothian that Mr. Gladstone will visit his constituents during the autumn recess. The Premier has stated that he feels under an obligation, having disap- pointed the electors at the beginning of the year, to fulfie his engagement as eariy as convenient. It is unders!ood that the visit will be made late in September or in October. THE VISIT OF ENGLISH JUDGES TO AMERICA. On I Tuesday the White Star steamer Celtic, sailed from the Mer- sey for New York, having on board a large number of pas- I sengers, amongst them being Lord Chief Justice Coleridge and Sir James Hannen, who have accepted invitations to be present at the annual meeting of the Bar Association of the State of New York. They were accompanied by Mr. P. Martin, Q C., M.P., Mr. Charles Russell, Q.C., M.P, the Hon. Mr. Coleridge, and Mr. James Chitty Hannen. SELLING CHILDREN.—A heartless case is reported from Oldham. On Monday evening a woman, abeut forty years of age, was seen in Curzon-street with two children, one in the arms and the other about three years old, walking by her side. It appeared that the woman wanted to sell her children, and thereupon a large crowd collected. She was successful in selling one child to a woman, who went off with her prize, for which she paid 6d., in a cab. The mother wanted to dispose of the other child, and at first asked 2d. for it. Ultimately she brought down her demand to id, but did not find a purchaser. "ALWAYS DRUNK "—At the Thames (London) Polk Court, on Monday, Margaret Kane, aged 30, SPAS charged with being drunk and disorderly outside the Letnan-street police station.—Mr. Saunders (to the prisoner) : You are charged with being drunk.—The Prisoner: Of course, I was drunk. lam always drunk, and I mean to get drunk as long as I live.—The Constable: She is newly out of prison. She has been here dozens of times.—The Pris.mer : I know I have, and I shall be here a lot more times.—Mr. Saunders: Well, you will go to prison this time for seven day.—The Prisoner: What! only seven days! I made sure you would have made it a month. Good luck to yer THE DYNAMITE CONSPIRACY.—At Liverpool, On Tues- day, James ArDermott, who had been arrested on landing from a Transatlantic steamer, was charged with coasphing with others to destroy public buildings and murder Govern- ment officials. The ev:dence of a metroplitan police officer showed that M‘Dermott was the hitherto missing companion of Dalton, one of the "dynemiters sentenced to penal ser- vitude for life at. Liverpool assizes. They were seen in- specting the Houses of Parliament, Lambeth Palace, the Local Government and other offices, and taking notes in re- gard to those buildings. Prisoner, who said he" courted the fullest inquiry," was remanded far a week. AN EXCURSION PARTY AT THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.—A remarkable scene took place at the House of Commons on Monday. Some time ago Mr. Arthur Peel, M.P. for War- wick, engaged to take 40 of his constituents over the House. On Monday morning he was surprised to learn that one train had left with 300 persons, and that another was leav- ing with an equally extensive freight. Upon their arrival at Westminster the impression for the moment was that they formed a provincial demonstration in favour of Mr. Brad- laagh, The members of the party, including many women who carried children in their arms, were conducted in relays by Mr. Peel through the principal apartments of the House. THE ARREST OF A MISSIONARY IN MADAGASCAR.—A private interview was granted by Lard Granville on Tues- day afternoon at the Foreign Office to a small deputation of the directors of the London Missionary Society. This society is naturally anxious in respect to its work in Mada- gascar, which the French attack upon that country has seriously checked, and especially in regard to the imprison- ment by the French Admiral of one of its agents, Mr. Shaw, who is engaged in missionary work at the bombarded port of ram itave. Lord Granville expressed to the deputation his satisfaction at hearing the view of the directors, and as- sured them that the Government had the case of Mr. Shaw under its particular and serious consideration. FATAL FIRE AT A LUNATIC ASYLUM: FIVE PERSONS BURNT TO DEATH.—A fire broke out early on Tuesday morning at a private lunatic asylum, which has been carried on for some years by Dr. Boyd, at Southall Park. The in- habitants of the neighbourhood were attracted by the shrieks of the inmates, who were at the windows endeavouring to find a means of escape. As many as could be got at were rescued as speedily as possible ; but, fortunately, the bulk of the patients were with their attendants at Brighton, Ramsgate, and other watering places. Teem were about 20 persons in the establishment at the time of the fire. The patients have been safely lodged in neighbouring houses. Dr. Boyd, his son, and three patients were burned to death. There were several of the inmates .severely injured. THE FORTH BRIDGE SCHEME.—A highly-favourable re- port by the Government inspectors regarding the erection of the bridges was presented at the half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of the Forth Bridge Railway Company on I Tnesday.—The Chairman (Sir James Falshaw) expressed his admiration of the manner in which the preparations had been made for building the vast structure. He remarked that quite a new town was being built at South Queen's Ferry, and in a few years they hoped to have a bridge that would be the admiration of the world. The statement of accounts showed that during the past half-year £47,607 had been expended in connection with the project, and in the report it was announced that within the next three months a call of Ll per share might be expected to be made. EXTRAORDINARY PRIVATIONS AT SEA.—The British brig Arctic has, it seems, been instrumental in succouring a Spanish vessel at sea under exceptionally hard circum- stances. As the Arctic was on her passage to Torre Viega she sighted a foreign vessel with distress signals flying. This was in latitude 41, longitude 2405, on the 22nd June. The Arctic remained by until a boat from the stranger came up to her. The men in the boat said their vessel was the Spanish brig Purisima Concepcion, and that she was going from New Orleans to Seville. The vessel had been a long time on the passage, and the provisions had all been ex- hausted. For the previous 15 days the men had no bread, and for the last five (lays no food of any description had been partaken of by any of the crew. T'ne Arctic's com- mander gave the men a supply of necessary provisions, which they took to their vessel, and then proceeded on her I voyage. SERIOUS RAtLWAi ACCIDENT: SEVEN PERSONS INJURED. —A very serious accident has just occurred at Halesowen Station, on the Great Western Railway. Alterations are now being made on the main line, and upon a passenger train being signalled from Old Hall, the home signal was left at "danger," On the train reaching the signal, the guard, whose name is Cresswell, slipped the carriage and the engine, and went on. Upon the stationmaster, how- ever, giving the signal of caution, the engine-driver applied the brake, the result being that the slipped coach came into violent collision with the engine. On the arrival of the train in the station it was discovered that seven passengers had been seriously injured, and some were now said to be suffering in a precarious state, most of them from contused wonnds and shocks. The injured ones are Jane Powell and Sarah Carley, Halesowen ; Mary Bordwick and William Bates, of Dudley and Win Cowman: and Alfred Hadley and Isaac Hodgkins, of Old Hill. THE ECCLESIASTICAL Cot:tem.—The report of the Royal Commission on the Ecclesiastical Courts, which was ap- pointed at the instance of the title Archbishop of Center- bury has been published. It recommends some very great and important changes. Under the Church Discipline Act there is no limit to the qualification of the prosecutors. Under the Public Worship Regulation Act the prosecutors !must be three aggrieved parishioners, resident for one year in the parish. But in practice this limitation has been found to be of no use whatever. The futility of this sup- posed safeguard .agaiest mere vexatious and malicious prosecutions has induced the commission to revert to the old plan, which leaves the right to prosecute perfectly open and unrestricted. This would throw the responsibility for the prosecution entirely on the bishop. The Archbishop of York dissents from this, and in signigg tbe report is com- pelled to record his dissent from it in two important par- ticulars. His grace, in the first place, objects to trust the bishops with the absolute discretionary power in stopping a prosecution all imitie. "Except with his (the bishop's) per- mission, the courts will be closed entirely to a layman, and no layman will have the right to appeal from this absolute decision, however great the wrong which be may conceive himself to have sustained." "To prevent the evils" of litigation "for the future something should be done to afford means of direction and arbitration, without resort to the courts." Therefore (says the archbishop), "let the bishop have power to make an order in all matters affecting the conduct of public worship, which shall be binding until I reversed by the Court of Appeal." PARLU.MENTARY REGISTRATION (IRELAND) BILL.—On the order for going into Committee on the Parliamentary Registration (Ireland) Bill, Mr. GIBSON protested Against the attempt of the Government to carry a bill of this char- acter at such a period in the session, and moved the rejec- tion of the measare.—Mr. TREVELYAN replied, and said the bill was not brought in to help one party or the other.—The motion for going into Committee was carried by 118 votes to 29, and the bill passed through Committee. THE BANKRUPTCY BILL--The next business was the Bankruptcy Rill, and, while calling attention to- the patron- age which this measure would place in the hands of the President of the Board of Trade, and asking for a Pledge that political considerations would not influence the ap- pointment of official receivers, Mr. Ritchie bore warm tes- timony to the skill with which the bill had been steered through the Grand Committee by Mr. Chamberlain. Mr. Dixon-Hartland and Mr. Stagg also bore testimony to the success of the Grand Committee, and to Mr. Chamberlain's masterly and businesslike management. Mr. Chamberlain himself expressed great satisfaction at the working of the Grand Committee system adding that he intended to leave the appointment of official receivers to a depatmental com- mittee, so that there could be no suspicion of political in- fluence in their appointment. Ultimately the report was agreed to, and the bill was read a third time. THE IRISH TRAMWAys BILL.—The House then took up the Irish Tramways Bill, the second reading of which was dismissed at some length, and the bill read a second time. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. TRAGEDY AT I.I7OANO.—A telegram from Lugano states that a tragic incident has just spread consternation among the tourists there. Count Dolfini, of Padua, has 15te17 come with his wife to reside in the picturesque little vii- lage of Melida, on the borders of the lake. They stayed at the Hotel Castelli, where they lived in veat state. A night or two since the Count approached M. Castelli, and without any warning fired twice at him with a revolver, wounding Lim mortally. The Count then fled, but was pursued and arrested. He has since ineffectually attempted suicide.

Inflamatory placards smuggled from Hungary, calculated, ro incite the people against the Jews, have been discovered in Ekaterinoslay. Further Jewish prosecutions are feared. In the ; recent anti-semetic outbreak at Ekaterinoslav, in - Russia, 14 persons were killed, 73 wounded, and 121 taken into custody. The property of more than 200 Jewish tradespeople, represent- ing, a value of 800,000 roubles, was plundered and des- stroyed. The town is now occupied by four regiments of infantry, a brigade of artiilery, Cures s)tniae of Cossacks and a squadron of cavalry. All trade, it is stated, is now suspended. According to a telegram from Berlin, it is stated on trust- worthy authority that negotiations have been opened between Vienna and Berl'n for the complete and absolute annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina by Austria. The Porte, it would appear, is also a party to the negetiations which so far are proceeding in a manner which gives satis- faction to the Vienna Cabinet. It is further alleged regard- ing the suggested annexation that several proposals for the Austro-Hungarian Delegation have been prepared by the •Austrian Cabinet, with a view to the settlement, not only of the railway questions affecting Bosnia and Herzegovina, but of the military institutions. • REPORTED SEDITION IN INDIA.-1110 Lahore Civil and 21filitaw Gazette is responsible for the statement that the Pun jaub postal authorities have lately seized a number of seditious letters addressed to certain parsons in Utnt itsir,and containing pieces of black cloth, which were to be worn, thp writer said, in mourning for Surrendroneth Bennerjee, the - Calcutta journalist, who was lately imprisoned for contempt_ of court. Distinctly seditious references are also made to • the approaching visit of Maharajah Dhuleep Singh to India. It seems to be not unlikely that some use may be made of , the Maharajah's name by disaffected persons. A telegram from Simla states that the prospect of his visit is causing _ considerable excitement among the native community, es- peeially the Sikhs, and that probably he will not be per- mitted to approach the Punjaub. ENGLISH LANDOWNERS IN MIERICA..—An American journal, in publishing statistics as to the immense quanti- ties of land held by English noblemen and others in the United States reports that Sir Edward Reed, M.P., owns no less than 2,000,000 acres; the Duke of Sutherla.;.,4oo,ooo ; Lord Dunmore, 100,000; and Lord Dunraven, ,000 acres. Messrs. Phillips, Marshall, and Co. own a farm Of 1,300,000 acres • the heirs of Col. Murphy, 1,100,000; li. Diston. 92,006,000 ; and the Standard Oil Co., 1,000,000 acres. It 'appears that nine men own a territory equal to that of New , Hampshire, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island combined. Then there are the great railroad, corporations, whose free • gifts of land from lavish Congresses amount to upwards of 200,000,000 acres. Eleven of these corporations have re- ceived 120,000,000 acres. The Northern Pacific Road had. grants amounting to 47.000,000 acres; and other grants made ranged from 1,000 000 acres upwards. AN ISLAND DESTROYED BY A VOLCANO.—A: communi- cation received from Panama, dated July 19, gives details of an immense volcanic outbreak at Ometepec, an island on Lake Nicaragua. For the pact three months a quiescent volcano has given signs that it was about to burst into activity. On June 19 the lava streamed from the new crater and ran in the direction of Las Piles. The sides of mountain became alive with fire as the lava poured down, sweeping with it trees, rocks, and earth, while the con- tinued bellowings and roarings brought terror to all who heard them. For several days the whole island was con- tinually quaking. Many inhabitants fled, and the authori- ties commenced the removal of everyone from the island. On the 24th the lava bed had covered up the road, and two, young men were buried under it. The molten matter con- tinued to pour out in an almost *interrupted stream. panic set in among the populace, rind schooners and boats, were sent to the island to transport the people to Granada, Rivas, and other cities. The lava flow on the 26th took a new direction, and cut off communication with the farms and pastures upon which the islanders depend for their living. The eruptions became terrible in their intensity, and led to the few remaining people fleeing to the main- land. Boiling lava, mud, ashes, and rocks now cover the sides of the mountain and the pleasant slepea which have been cultivated for centuries. THE Irrstnauscriois IN SPAlN,—Official telegrams from Madrid on Saturday give an assurance that the insurrection in Spain is entirely at an end, and that eomplete tranquility prevails throughout the Peninsula. A manifesto, printed at Lisbon by the leaders of the revolutionary movement, states that the programme of the insurgents was "The Spanish Republic, the Constitution of 1869, the abolition of slavery in Cuba, compulsory military sera-ice, and a great number of administrative reforms." The Madrid corres- pondent of the Times says that the Spanish Foreign Minis- ter, who bad to travel though Portugal on his way from Galicia, was enabled to communicate to his colleaguee de- tails of the conspiracy :—" Civiliane were rigidly ex- cluded from any knowledge of what was going on, as well as common soldiers, corporals, and officers above the rank of lieutenant colonel. Each batch of conspirators numbered ten, nine out of this number only k:;owing separately, not collectively, their chief ; and he, in turn, only knowing the decursion of another ten nien, from whom his orders were received. The oath excluded, all civilians, hut not re- tired officersewho appear to have taken a leading part in the movement. N 1 hen King Alleuso came to the throne he found an vecess of 22,000 officers in the army. The only way to remedy this state of things was to atop promotion and to place the greater nuraher of the officers on the re- setve list. Both steps wero bitterly resented by subalterns and sergeants in active service, and by retired superior officers. Hence the military conspiracy which has lent itself to Baia Zorilla in consUeration of the funds provided to. carry it on."
TRANSFER OF lICENSE.—The license of the Grifin Earlestowa, was transferred to Charles Sowler, by the magistrates at the Nzwton Town Hall, on Saturday last.

In the Quiver (Messrs. Cassell and Co., Limited) for August appears the first of a charming series of Papers,under the head of" Papers from Dovedale," by" The Rector," en- titled " At the Study Window," and forming a most refresh- ing moreeau of summer reading. A new story, entitled " Doddleliins," which is spoken of as bAng one of the most delightful sketches of child character ever written is also commenced. Mr. Robert Barnes, who excels as a painter of child-life, has been engaged to draw the full-page illustra- tion. "My Grandfather's Mistake," by Edward Garrett, is a story told in the author's mist pi:: acing style. The Rev. Prebendary Jackson, in " The Seven Churches of Asia," shows how fully the Scriptural prophecies have been ful- filled. The Rev. P. B. Power, author of "The ' I wills' of the Psalms,' contributes one of his characteristic papers on " The Soul's Longings." "Sonic Providential deliverances," relates some authentic instances of remarkable escapes from death or danger. " The Orphan Homes of Scotland," is an account of the Orphanages at the Bridge of Weir, through which 239 inmates passed last year, who filled afterwards places of usefulness in Canada and elsewhere. " Doubly Blind" contains some highly interesting passages this month, and there are short stories and numerous other papers for Sunday and general reading.— The contributions to the Family Mayn:ine (by the same publishers) comprise " A Persian Orgy in Cairo," descrip- tive of a curious and and barbarous custom, from the pen of an eye-witness. " The Water Babies of our Canals," by Mr. Maurice Adams, F.A.S., deals with the juvenile portion of the canal population, giving much valuable information on the subject. " Flower Gatherers and Flower Gathering in North Notts," introduces the reader to a very pretty and interesting industry in that county. The " Special Cor- respondent " of the magazine continues her researches on behalf of her lady readers, and points out still further very useful sources of remunerative work for gentlewomen. The making of ices at home has always been a difficulty with most housewives. A practical paper on this subject, by Miss L. Heritage, former priz a essayist on domestic economy, will be read with gratitude by many ladies. ' "Only Middling," is the despondent answer often received in resp',nse to our" How do you do ?.' and in this number "The Family Doctor " takes up this sad echo, and brightens us up with hopeful words seasoned by a little wholesome and practicable advice. " The Fair Maid of Cherbury "is by the author of that charming story, "A Moonbeam Tangle." " Blocked in a Tunnel " is also a very thrilling incident, founded, we believe, on an actual occur- rence. We have received three holiday handbooks dealing with " Holland," "The Moselle," and " The Ardennes," which will be found of great value to intending excursionists. They are very pleasantly written, beautifully illustrated, and each contains some excellent hints. They are edited by Mr. P. Lindley, of the Great Eastern Railway Company, by whom they are published. LEIGH IN THE EIGHTEENTH CENTURY.—ThiS volume is from the pen of Mr. Josiah Rose, a well-known local anti- quary, Fellow of the Royal Historical Society, hon..member of the Virginia Historical Society, &c. The period dealt with embraces the years from 1689-1813. and we need scarcely say that the -book contains a great deal of informa- tion of much interest locally. Many ancient documents are reproduced for the benefit of those who have a taste for their perusal ; and the old accounts which are set forth in detail throw a flood of light on the doings of our forefathers. On the whole the book is very entertaining, it reveals a vast amount of research on the part of the author, as well as much care bestowed in its compilation, and it reflects the highest credit on his-literary attainments.

On Wednesday afternoon, while the four-horse coach which runs ,iluring the tourists' season between Lockearn- head and Crieff was near the former place the splinter bar , broke, and the vehicle was upset. Three lady passengers were so seriously injured that they were unable to continue their journey, and the others were severely shaken and stunned. BRUTAL ILLUSAOF OF A. PARALYTIC WIFE.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Wednesday, William Heeson was charged with assaulted his wife, Catherine, on Menday.—He pleaded guilty, but said if he hid not been drunk he would not have done it.—The complainant, who appeared to be ' suffering from paralysis, and had to be supported by two officers, said her husband struck her on the shoulder, knocked her down, and then kicked her. ller mouth WAS swollen, but she could not say whether it had been done by the fall or by a kick from her husband. She did not wish. to do him any injury, as he was a good husband but for the drink.—Superintendent Johnston said there was no previous conviaion against Heeson, but he should like the Bench to hear P.C. Radcliffe about the way he Mused his wife. She r zany Might to have protection.—Tho Benob, however, \thought P.C. Radcliffo's evidence would li. ot be strictly relative to the case. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, AUGUST 18, 1883.

The House of Commons was nnPc/Jay occupied for the most part with two Irish measures, both of which deserve to be speedily placed upon the statute book; whether they will be so or not remains to be seen. The first had reference to Parliamentary registration in Ireland, and its object, stated briefly, is to secure to every Irishman the right to the franchise conferred upon him in 1868, on the same footing in regard to re- gistration as that upon which every English- man and Scotchman enjoys his vote. It requires but very little sagacity to discover, that if the mode of registration followed in England and Scotland is good for the electors cf those two countries, the adoption of the same principle in Ireland is not likely to do much, if any, harm; and for this very cogent reason, probably, the bill meets the general approval of all patties. As a matter of fact it was passed by the House of Commons three years ago without opposition; though when sent up to the peers their lordships followed their usual custom in regard to Irish matters, and threw the bill out. In the present instance the measure has encountered some little opposition in the Lower House, not to its principle, which was never assailed, but on account of the late period -of the ses- sion which the Government had chosen to submit it to the judgment of the House. An attempt was made to defeat the bill on this very inadequate ground, but it failed, and the measure has been read a third time. We are afraid, however, that the bill awaits from the Peers the fate it met on a former occasion. Indeed, the fiat has gone forth that its rejec- tion will be moved by some noble lord on the front Opposition bench, and if the motion is persisted in and supported by the full strength of the Conservative party, there is no hope of this act of simple justice becoming law at pre- sent. Ireland will in that event have to en- dure a little longer the grievance which the bill is designed to remedy; and it would be well that the Irish people should note who is re- sponsible. We need scarcely say that the only sure remedy for such misfortunes as that predicted is the total abolition of the Upper Chamber as a legislative assembly. This, of course, is not yet a question within the range of practical politics, yet it approaches that stage the more the peers place themselves in antagonism to the will of the people, and when the question does come to the front, Irishmen will then, if not before, have an op- portunity of marking their appreciation of the conduct of their Lordships towards Ireland. With the view of facilitating legislation, it was suggested in the House of Commons the other night that one or more Government measures should be introduced into the House of Lords early in the session; but judging from the manner in which their lordships mutilate some bills and contemp- tuously throw out others, it may be open to doubt whether any advantage whatever could result from following such a course as that hinted at. To us it appears to be one very much to be deprecated. At the same time we can understand that the total extinction of the House of Lords would be a great gain. The second of the two bills to which we have alluded is what is known as the Tramways and Public Corhpanies (Ireland) Bill. The introduction of this measure, which has now been read a second time, has been described by an Irish member as "the most important event in the industrial development of the country that has occurred since the Union," and he adds that should it fail to become law an irreparable misfortune will have befallen Ireland. The bill, which,

except in one or two particulars, has elicite- general approval, has a threefold 013- object, but a common' aim, namely, to Per- manently relieve distress and to advance the prosperity of the country. The first part of the bill sanctions the extension of steam tramways, by which it is hoped to provide labour where it is most wanted, while at the same time the means of conveyance will be improved and better facilities afforded for developing the resources of the country. M the tram lines are completed, districts noW neglected will be brought into closer com- munication with each other, and channels will thus be opened up for the sale of the produce of the soil as well as for its better and more convenient transit to other par?. The State, however, in now giving material aid towards the promotion of industry, makes it incumbent upon the local authorities td assist. These local authorities will be the promoters of the tramways, and half the dividends which the promoters in conjunction with the various baronies may guarantee investors will be allowed by the State, provided the sum so payable does net exceed four per cent on the whole capital. The amount which the bill authorises the Treasury to guarantee in this way ls £4.0,000 a year, representing at two Per cent. a capital of two millions sterling, a sum which ought to be adequate and td give a healthy impetus to commercial enter" prise. The second part of this bill IS designed to assist persons desirous of egg" grating. There are so many persons id Ireland anxious to emigrate, but cannot do so without help, that the Government feel, themselves justified in devoting £lOO,OOO to this object. This portion of till bill is one which has awakeneu some opposition from Mr. PARNELL and his followers, who look upon the emigration proposals with considerable suspicion. They insinuate the ob- ject of the Government is to force the people out of the country against their will, though there is no such intention. Mr. PAW , NELL and his friends favour a scheme for the removal of the people from one part of OP,. country to another, and they contend that 0 half the £xoo,ooo were devoted to that par- pose, then the Irish leaders would have ao opportunity of proving what they believe thei can fairly and practically prove during the coming winter, namely, that it is possible to migrate or re-settle families from the conges- ted districts in such a way as to enable them to live and thrive in Ireland as well as theY can in America. It would be a pity if aP opportunity were not given for testing this point. The only object the .Government call have is to do the best for the country and the, people, and if some practical scheme al migration is placed before them, it will, as, Mr. Trevelyan has promised, be entertained' At the same time it would be wrong of the Government to withhold assistance from those anxious to emigrate, but who have na! the wherewithal; and let it be rememberea that it is only those who are willing to einv grate the Government propose to assist. There is no desire to force the peoples as is erroneously supposed, to leave th.e country. By the third part of the bill it is proposed to practically extend the Par,: chase Clauses of the Land Law Act, whicil have so far been productive of but few sales. Companies who satisfy the Land Commission of their intention to buy land for the purpos.e, of re-selling it to tenants will by this part of the bill be permitted to purchase from the owner on the sumo tct Ins as are now granted to occupying tenants—that is to say, bypaying a quarter of the purchase money and leaving three-quarters on mortgage. It is to be hoped that this will have the effect• af stimulating the exchange of land, and placing it ultimately in the hands of the tenants, whose great hope must lie in them becoming owners. One objection to this bill is worth noting, and it is one by Mr. GIBSON to effect that there is no necessity for the bib now because there is no sp cial distress ; byt surely one of the objects of this sort of leg's' lation should be to avert distress, and we rather think that if th,: Government of whien Mr. GIBSON was a member had acted upon this principle, Ireland would never have fallen into the condition of discontent and disorder from which it is only now recovering. Wre sincerely hope that this last bill, whatever befalls the other at present, may become la'v this session, for it is one destined to be pill- ductive of great and lasting good ; and NO believe that even the Peers will hesitate be- fore damaging or throwing out so useful 3 measure.
