CAMDEN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNOORN.—The scholars at- tending this school had their annual treat to Sutton Hall on Thurday. Under the care of the superintendents and the secretaries they left the rail way station at two o'clock in a special train, accompanied by the band, and the weather being very favourable for out-door amusements, spent a pleasant aternoon in the green fields. Tea was pro- vided for the children. PR,CPOSED YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION FOR WIDNES.—At the forthcoming conference of the West Mid- land District of Young Men's Association, to be held at Liverpool, the 'advisability of establishing a Young Men's Christian Association is to be considered. Some years ago such an association existed in Widnes, but the slender support it received did not justify the committee in con- tinuing their labours. and it came to a premature end. That an institution of this kind is needed is a satement that requires no enforcing, for the town possesses neither reading room nor library, and the greater portion of the workingmen pass their evenings at the street corners or in the public- houses. A Row IN THE BLUE BALL, Rtmootor. At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Mr. A. Thomas and Capt. Hazlehurst, George Buckingham, alias Partington, was brought up under a warrant charged with having on the 11th October, 1882, been guilty of disorderly conduct in the Blue Ball Inn, Fryer-street, and refusing to leave when re- quested to do so. Robert Dwyer, the landlord, gave evi- dence to the effect that on the day named a sailor named Blackmore was treating the company to drink, but did, net ask the prisoner to participate in the general treat. The prisoner thereupon struck Blackmore, and created a great disturbance. He declined to leave when requested, and was ejected.—The Bench fined him 20s and costs, 7s 6d, or a month's hard labour. PARENTS AND THEIR ERRING CHILDREN AT WIDNES.— On Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Thomas Bate was summoned to show cause why he should not contribute to- wards the support of his son, who is an inmate of the Liver- pot Industrial school. When the boy was committed the defendant was not in a position to pay, but Inspector Bar- nett proved that he was now earning 35s per week, and Superintendent Barker applied for an order for is 6,1 per week against the defendant.—Granted.—Michael Kelly, who has two children in an industrial school, was ordered to pay is 6d per week towards the maintenance of each child.--An order for the payment of £4 lie 8d was made upon John Bowe who was to that extent in arrears for the maintenance of his two children in an industrial school. ALLEGED ASSAULT ON A DOMESTIC SERVANT AT DITTON. —At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Henry Pen- nington, a young man, was charged with assaulting Selina Wilson, a domestic servant.—Mr. Swift appeared for the defence.—Complainant stated that on Sunday, the 22nd July, when she was walking along Ball-lane on her way home, she was followed by the defendant, who struck her, threw her to the gtound, and behaved indecently. She screamed and the defendant ran away.—Complainant called a woman who said she was within a yard of the parties when the alleged assault took place. The complainant and de- fendant were walking together and she saw no assault com- mitted, and that the complainant was no worse.—Mr. Swift called three witnesses for the defence, named R. Shakeshaft, Mrs. Middleton, and Mrs. Broome.—The Bench dismissed the case.

WIDNES DESERTERS FROM THE IRISH ARTILLERY MILITIA.—Phillip Keogh, about 30 years of age, was brought up at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, charged with absenting himself from the training of the 'lth brigade Royal Artillery North Irish Wicklow Militia on I the 7th June, 1879.—P.5. Macgregor stated that at half- past three .'clack on Saturday afternoon he apprehended the prisoner in the Widnes Alkali Works, and charged him with being a deserter. He admitted the offence.—Sergeant Dempsey, of the Royal Artillery, proved the prisoner's absence, and wished him to be dealt with summarily.—The Bench fined the prisoner £2, and costs £2 6s 6d, or, in de- fault, a month's impriaonment.--Thomas Martin, a young fellow, and a corporal in the regiment, was charged with a similar offence.—He pleaded that he had not received notice, but Sargeant Dempsey proved that notices were served. Ho I gave the prisoner a good character.—The Bench imposed a tine of £2, and costs £2 6a 6J, or, in default, a month's im- prisonment.

RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE: HANDSOME Green—The monthly meeting was held on Thursday, under the presidency of Mr. W. Handley. There were present Messrs. Meadowcroft, Like, Riley, Rhodes, and Brookes (secretary).—The Libratian reported that the library was open 12 days duting the month. Tire total number of books borrowed were 923, classified as follows :—Theology 16, political econceny, law, &c., 4; history, travels, bio- graphy, 85; science and art, 29; poetry and the drama, 9; prose fiction, 743; miscellaneous, 37. The receipts were Ll 7s 11d. Accounts amounting to Ll 3s 111 were passed for payment.—The Chairman remarked that recently a pub- lic meeting in Bath had decided by a large mei), ity not to adopt the Free Libraries Act, and the Subscription Library in the city had suspended operations. The volumes had been distributed amongst the gentlemen entitled tel them. and Mr. Isaac Pitman had received 2,000 books. He had given 500 of them to the Birmingham Free Library. and was offering 50 to each of the other free libraries in the country. He had written to the Runcorn Free Library ask- ing them to select 50 volumes from a catalogue he for- warded —Mr. Lake moved that Mr. Pitman's offer be grate- fully accepted, and it was carried.—The Chairman observed that the committee's year of office concluded that day, and the meeting-terminated. TEMPERANCE MISSION AT WIDNES.—Miss Griffiths, of West Bromwich, has during the past week been conducting a temperance mission for the Good Templars of the Sun- beam Temple in Widnes, and her labours have been very successful. The lady commenced on Sunday afternoon when she preached a sermon to a large congregation in Oak- land-street Wesleyan Chapel. In the evening also she preached, and on Monday evening a public meeting was held under the presidency of the Rev. R. Harper, who ex- pressed the opinion that the tints was coming when Christians generally would become total abstainers. and it behoved Methodists to be to the front.—Miss Griffiths de- livered an earnest address in which she declared the tem- perance question to be a women's question, inasmuch as they were the most aff?cted by the misery which drunken- ness caused. She described the manifold evils which a craving for strong drink entailed upon home and kindred, and appealed for sympathy and help in the temperance cause. On Tuesday evening a meeiug was held in Oekland-erreet Wesleyan School, Mr. T. S. Swale presiding on this occasion. The Chairman and Miss Griffiths delivered appro- priate speechee. Music played a prominent pert in the evening's proceedings, the children and choir, und. r the conductorship of Mr. Betnev, rendering in fine style several hymns and odes. Mr. Price was at the hermonium. A third meeting was held on Wednesday evening in the Primitive Methodist Cha el, Simm's Cross. There was a large audience, and the Rev. J. Morton, of Warrington, presided. Miss Griffiths was again the principal -speaker, and delivered another of her interesting addresses. The choir sang a number of appropriate hymns, and Mre. Locke and Miss Casey sang a duet. RUNCORN RIFLE VOLUNTEERS. With the rest of the Earl of Chester's rifles, the Runcorn companies have just had a week in tent on Conway Marsh, and have on for themselves special mention by their soldierly bearing and general good conduct. Unfortunately the weather was of a most boisterous and stormy character, ann owing to the rain, the full number of drills were not gone through. The wind on several °exactions blew across the camping ground with great fury, and it was by no meanc a rare occurrence for a tent to collapse upon-the heads of the occupants during the night time, when dhey had to turn out and set to work and re-erect it under eonditions which were by far from haliday like, and gave them a glimpse of aesoldier's life under ad- verse circumstances Many of the volunteers, too, were glad to rcll themselves in their blankets without disrobing, in order to keep themselves warm, but-t is pleasing to learn that all difficulties were surmounted and no cases of illness have resulted. The inspection of thefeattalion took place on Friday last week, and the Colonel expressed the opinion that the F and G companies presented the smartest appear- ance and were the best drilled of the whole of the troops he bad had the pleasure of inspecting, thus aonveying a CM- pliment not only to the men but to the officers, and one which is theroughly deserved. A. tent in G Company was awarded the firet,prize for being ,the most neat and reepectablean the ground. On Saturday evening a large crowd of people assembled at the railway station to welcome the volunteers on their reearn, and as they emerged from the platform they were greeted with en- thusiasm. The companies were under the eemmand of Captain Hazelhurst, Lieutenants Timmins, Joule, Rhodet, and instructor Player, Captain Joiiiffe having had to leave his company at Frodsham. The men formed in front of the railway station and were addressed by Captain Haelehurst, I who thanked them for being in camp in such large numbers and trusted that in another year they would be Wet() put even a larger force on the ground. It was exceedingly creditable:to the men that they had, with only one or two exceptiona,conducted themselvee with such praiseworthy propriety. They had presented while in camp a soldieriT and efficient appearance, and bad deeply impressed their Colonel, who had informed him that the F and G come parries were the .eleaenst, smartest,and best drilled on parade. He was pleased that they merited these words of praise,and hoped that they would continue to boll their high standard in the battalion. He regretted that owing to no fault of the , officers there had been a failure in the arrangements on the day of arrival which had slightly militated agalusA the comfort of the men but he should person- ally take care next year that they should not suffer from a similar inconvenience. Their quarters should be quite as good as those provided for the officers, and he would see that there should not ha cause for the slightest complaint. Captain Hazelhurst then bade the men good night and departed by train. Lieutenant Timmins then tack command, and to the strains of "Oar Jack's coat /awn? .10-day," the ToNnteera marched to the drill hall. •

SONS OF TEMPBRANCH, RUNCORN.—The members of the Lifeboat Crew division of this order are already reaping the fruits of their recent successful demonstration. At the !sat meeting 10 persons were nominated members, while 22 others were proposed for membership. NELSON-STREET WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RITNCORN. —The Rev. A. Roebuck preached two sermons in Camden Sunday School, on Sunday last, in connection with the above school. In the afternoon Mr. G. Hazlehurst conduc- ted a children's service. The children and the choir sang special music during the day. The collections amounted to £l6. - -

- - ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.--11 Will be observed from our advertising columns that a meeting is to be held at the Town Hall, Chester, on Monday, the 27th inst.— ender the presidency of his Grace the Duke of Westminster —for the purpose of taking steps to induce the Royal Agricultural Society to hold their show of 1885 in that city. The cordial co-oporation of all classes will be required if the object aimed at is to be achieved, and we hope the approaching meeting will,therefore,be thoroughly representa- tive.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL SCHEME.—A special meeting of the Provisional Committee appointed by the pro- moters of the Manchester Ship Canal Scheme was held on Tuesday, at the offices, 70a, Market-street, 'Winchester. Mr. Daniel Adamson presided, and submitted a lengthy report of the proceedings which have been taken with a view to obtain the sanction of Parliament to the cairyiag out of the scheme. A long discussion followed, during which commu- nications were submitted from gentlemen who have volun- tarily offered further pecuniary assistance towards the east of the prosecution of the scheme in the next session of Parliament. Ihe committee came, however, to the conclu- sion that it is not desirable to take any action in that direc- tion until the accounts up to the present date leave been closedf and until a meeting of the subscribers has been called. Directions were given that the steps necessary to secure these objects should be at once taken. The com- mittee, who will probably meet again early next week, will, we are informed, call a meeting of the subscribers as Boon as a complete financial statement can be presented to them. Some little time, however, must necessarily elapse before this can be done.

div.head: PRIMITIVE ME IsIIODISM IN UNCOR N. LECTURE ON " LIVINGSTONE."
div.p: PRIMITIVE ME IsIIODISM IN UNCOR N. LECTURE ON " LIVINGSTONE."

In aid of the funds of a bazaar, which is to be held in September, with the object of defraying tile exp-nses in connection with the heating apparatus recently placed in the chapel, two sermons were preached in the Greenway- road Primitive Methodist Chapel, on Sunday, by the Rev. D. S. Prosser, of Walkden. There were good congregations, and collections were taken at each service. On Monday evening a moderate attendance assembled in the sacred edi- fice to hear Mr. Prosser lecture on "David Livingstone." The chair was occupied by Mr. J. Humphreys. Devotional ' exercises having been conducted by the Rev. J. Pickwell, the Chairman briefly introduced the lecturer, who dealt with his subject in a most able and eloquent manner. He described Livingstone as a star of the first magnitude. No name of our time commanded greater or more universal admiration than did his, and all nations united to do homage to.shis greatness and goodness, and paid tribute to his nobility and worth. Referring to Livingstone's labours in Africa, the lecturer said Livingstone left England for Africa in the year 1840, being then 25 years aid. At that time Africa was the subject of much speculation; the , interior was thought to be one vast desert waste; and to Livingstone was due the honour and fame of having rollEd back the darkness. He dissipated the mystery that gathered about the source of the Nile, disproved the theory Oat central Africa was a desert waste, comected that im- mense country. with the civilised world, proved it to be teeming with population, rich in mineral treasure, possessed of nearly every form of vegetable and animal life, abound- in magnificent rivers, in towering mountains, and in hn- it-lenge lakes. In future time, when its races were endowed with the bleesings of civilisation and Christianity, Africa would know how much it was indebted to the tireltss toil, the undoubtthle will, and the heroic zeal of Christ-like Livingstone. The Lecturer, in graphic language, then des- cribed in detail Livingstone's wonderful achievements as missionary, travellet, explorer, and concluded with a poetical perwation. In the course of his lecture Mr. Prosser was frequently applaud,d, and at its conclusion he was accorded a heal-1y vote of thanks, on the motion of the Rev. J. Pickwell, seconded by Mr. Palin, A similar com- pliment was paid the Chairman, on the motion of Mr. Pick- well, seconded by Mr. Spender.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY FATALITY TO fi,.N
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY FATALITY TO fi,.N
OLD MAN AT RUNCORN.

On Saturday afternoon last, an accident of an extraordin- ary nature occurred at the 0;c1 Quay Docks, Runcorn, ending fatally to one of the men concerned. It appears that after a flat had passed through the locks, the gates, in con- sequence of some obstruction, would not close, and the men at the winch—Thomas Royle and Joseph Siddelfy— determined to flush the lock. To prevent the gate from moving back whilst this was being done, a wooden wedge was placed between the teeth of the cog wheel. The means adopted were successful, the obstruction was removed, and the men had just seized the handles of the winch prepara- tory to closing the gAtes, when the wedge sin ushed. Tne preesure of water on the gates caused them to shut suddenly, and the handles of the winch whirled rapidly round, eending the men who held them with great violence away. Siddeley was thrown to the ground, tut he was unh rt, and rising he saw Royle on his back in a dying state, with a gash two inches long and three-quarters of an inch deep on the back of his head, from which blood was flowing freely. Siddeley immediately ran for a doctor, whilst Joeeph Key, a fellow-workman, supported Royle's herd on hisknee. The injured man expired, however, in a few minutes, and was thee removed to his home in Ellesmere- street. He had attained the age of 72, but was bale and hearty. On Monday after- noon Mr. T. J. Ridgway, the coroner, held an inquest on the body at the Commercial Inn, Bridge-street, Mr. F. Fairhurst 1 being the foreman of the jury. Mr. Meadowcroft represented I the Bridgewater Navigation Company, Limited. Before cemmencing the inquiry the jury viewed the scene of the fatality.—Evidence bearing out the facts narrated above was given by James Royle, shipwright, Swinton, near Man- chester; Joseph Siddeley, dock labourer, of 32, Wellington- , street; and Edward Key, 11, Al b rt-street.—Same doubt existed as to bow deceased received his wound, and Key was of opinion that his head Celine in contact with a flag, and was not struck by the handle. This was generally ac- cepted.—Several members of the jury observed that the cog wheel was much worn, but the workmen agreed that a i worn mg wheel was much less liable to break, and worked better than a new one, and in this view they were borne out by Mr. Lea, a juryman. who ad led that doubtless the sharp end of the cogs had cut the wedge.—The Coroner said be was unfavourably impressed with the winch, but after hear- ing the statements of the witneeees and Mr. Lea he was satisfied that it was in proper working order.—lt was sug- gested that an iron wedge should be used.—After a short conferenctein private the jury returned a verdict of " Ac- cidental deetb."—The body of the deceased was interred at the Parish Church on Wednesday afternoon. It was fol- lowed to the: grave by about 100 relatives and employes of the Bridgewaer Navigation Comer:ay, among the number being the fotlowing:—Mr. J. Meadewcroft, Captain Garnett, Captain Edwards, Messrs. Robert Boyle, John Rnyle, Thos. Royle, Jamecaoyle, D. Ocklestone, William Pendlebury, Joseph SiddeZey, Edward Key, Ralph Peacock, William Cockup, Thomas Walker, J. Percivat, Yates, and John , Garnett. Church-street was lined with spectators whilst I.the procession passed; aft. observing a most decorous be- -havionr. The Rey. Mr. Edwards conducted the burial' service.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

WINDING UP THE SESSION.-LEISURE AND HURRY. - THE WHITEBAIT DINNER. - THE WOODEN SPOON.-" WHO GOES HOME ?"-THE "USUAL TIME."-THE COST 'OF LAND TRANSFER. A HUMAN VECiETABLE:-A MISCHEVIOUS CURE FOR COLIC.-LECTURING NEWSPAPER EDITORS. PRE "STANDARD" AND THE "DAILY NEWS".- THE ART UNION OF ENGLAND. LONDON, THURSDAY.

Parliament is now rapidly winding up its business, and soon the day will come when the cry of " Who goes homer, will echo for the last time this year through the deserted lobby. The rapidity with which work is now being rattled off contrasts strangely with the dilatory procedure of the earlier months of the session. There is a good deal of talk about the evil wrought to the public service by this haste. But en the whole, there is no doubt that the greater evil lies in the other extreme. What is wanted is the happy medium, which prebably will never be found as long as Parliament is comducted on the basis of Party. The ex- planation of what is taking place in the house just now is that the Opposition have retired from the contest. They have fought through the revolving weeks, and have succeeded in preventing the rapid acretion of work. Now they are drawn away by various influences, and the Minis- teralists, victoriously occupying the battle ground, do their work. In the last days Sir H. Wolff has re-appeared with opposition to the Scotch Local Government Board Bill, reminding the House of what might have happened, even at this period, had Lord Randolph Churchill been in his place. But the fight is literally over, and it is settled beyoud doubt that the Government mill carry their main measures, and will have a fair programme of accomplished work to chew. The Ministerial Whitebait dinner took place as usual on Wednesday night. But it was not a very lively affair, and bore about it many signs of growing decrepitude. One accidental circumstance of depression was found in the weather. It was a cold wet autumnal night, and the Thames is not a cheerful highway in such circumstances; more- over there were many conspicuous absentees. Mr. Gladstone has begun to plead the privileges of age, and begs that he may be excused. Then there had been some misunder- standing about the day. The dinner usually takes place on the Wednesday preceding the prorogation, and Wednesday next had been looked forward to as the proper occasion. For some reason Lord Richard Grosvenor, who has the arrange- ment under his hand, fixed Wednesday in this week, and it found many Ministers engaled. Three—Sir William Harcourt, Sir Charles Dilke, and Mr. Courtney—had dinner parties, at their own .houses; the one social engagement from the fulfilment of which a man cannot be excused. They were accordingly absent. But the dinner was, it is said. sufficiently merry, Lord Granville's company being in itself almost sufficient to meet that end. It is the correct 1 thing on this occasion for Ministers to go to the very extreme of abandonment of official manner, and to give themselves up to cheerfullest conversation. There is one Ii tie ceremony known as the presentation of a wooden I spoon. This is a gift designed for the Minister who has most conspicuously failed in carrying the measures com- mitted to his charge. This year, as last, Mr. Dodson was the pleased recipient of the gift. In fact, as Mr. Dodson has now been many years in Ministerial office, he must have quite a collection of wooden spoons.

I have mentioned the cry of "Who goes home?" Per- haps, as it does not appear in the Parliamentary report, it may be useful to explain that every day the moment the speaker leaves the chair on the adjournment of the House, the principal doorkeeper rising from his seat cries aloud, "Who goes home?" Strangers who have chanced to be in the lobby at this particular time may have heard the curious cry. But there is another, which with many years' pretty intimate acquaintance with Parliamentary manners I never happened to hear till a few weeks ago. This was the cry, uttered by the doorkeeper as he hurries away from his post, "The usual time ! " These are curious and interesting relics of bygone ages, and illustrate the ingraining Conservatism of the House of Commons. I have never heard any expla- nition of either; but it is probable that the first was in its day useful in bringing together members going the same way home, and glad of each other's company. When Lou- don was by oil lamps swinging at murky corners, and foot-pads abounded, it was well for hon. members wending their way homewards to keep together. "The usual time" is obviously an intimation that the House will meet at that I same time on the following day.

It_is to be hoped that next year the Government will not enly be able to bring in a bill cheapening the transfer of land, but would find 4ime to carry it out. A case has re- cently come und,-r my notice which illustrates, I don't know to what extent in extreme degree, the almost prohibitive cost of purchasing land. I friend of mine bought in a re- mote country town a few roods of land whereon to build a house. The purchase money was £l5O. He has now re- ceived a bill for the legal costs, which amount to within a ; few shillings of £lB, more than sue-eighth the total cost of the property! The transfer of a similar value in the funds ' or in ordinary shares 'quoted on the Stock Exchange, would not have been more than 15s. In addition to tbis charge, delays in carrying out the transfer deferred possession for upwards of six months.

One of the old houses near the river is again in the market. It has a long history of which the latest chapter is the most melancholy and the most weird. Here tor many years lived, if it could be called living:, one of the richest men in the kingdom. He was stricken by some fell and mysteriout disease which attacked both brain and body, left him in a condition much.nearer akin to a vegetable than any other living thing. The greatest mercy that could have befallen him would ha,ve been a speedy death. But his continued existence was of vast money value, and be was accordingly kept alive by all the arts that medical skill .could devise, watched over and cared for with a loving kindness that could not be rmceeded by a mother for her child. Science and skill triumphed for many years, and it was only the other day that the poor thing passed away.

An instructive story comes back to the House of Corn- moos from members who have already set forward on holi- day travel. Two were journeying by the through train from Paris to Geneva on their way to Switzerland. Tney bad a coupe. and had made every arrangement for a pleasant journey. They dined at the Lyons Station in Paris, a little too hastilyiit is to be fearol, for before they had gone very far one of them began to complain of colic His com- panion, who with parliamentary aptitule combines profound scientific knowledge, was equal to the occasion. " The best thing you can do," he says, "is to take 90110 carbon- ate of soda. I have some in iny bag." The patient grate- fully accepted the offer, and the doctor protlueing a glass bottle drom his dressing bag, poured out a handful of the contents., which his friend chewed and swallowed. " How do youleel cow ?" "A little better," said the patient. "Better have another dose," said the doctor, end another handful disappeared. The patient slowly but -surely got better, and spent quite a pleasaut night in the train. When they arrived at Geneva in the morning the 'doctor, opening his dressing hag to get his tooth powder, founs: that the bottle in which it had been was empty, whilst another small bottle of the same sies holding carbonate of soda was fait! Lord Richard Grosvenor says that thliiserves the hon. member sight. If he had been in his place in the House of Commons voting on the Scotch Local Governtnent Board 'Bill he would not have had the colic or been oared by copious doses of tooth powder.

The access of anger and indigration which last year beat about the Standarti has apparently subsided in the Conser- vative party. Mr. Mudford having ventured to conduct his journal according to bis own light, there went up a horrified shriek from the Conservatives, subsiding into a rumble of muttered threats when they found the editor was not to be shaken. In olden timna when the Staxdard was known as "Mrs. Gamp," it was simustorned feebly to flatter round the Conservative leaders,acd servilely echo their sentiments. The new editor changed all that, and by his independnce and courage raised the Staxdard to a position of influence second to none in the London Press. With this added political influence came increased commercial prosperity, a circulation nearly doubled, and unlimited advertisements. The wild threats of starting a new morning paper which should be the rival of the Standard and the acknowledged exponent of Conservative principles resulted in the retitle- r tion of the Horning Peat to a penny, which was a fair illustration of the business acurnen of the blusterer,. The kind of people who read the Morging Posit could well aft_srd to ptv threepence. To reduce it to a penny wile either to alter its characteristics in order to suit the new circle it addre:sed, or to leave it as it was and whilgt lying two-
pence a copy gaining no new circle of readers. lam not sure which course has been adopted, but it certainly has not harmed the Stanclaiq.

In degree the s.-itne kind of ofticioug ant impertinent meddling successfully resisted by the AS'taArlo?..7. :s j:ist now, hustlirg over the hte-ol of the Dai?.?, _lrw3. .1' ilurnal whilst frequently nale th 3 receptac!e of the cri nee of many, &clines therefore, or for ;my oth• r reA,o to be the mere 0r,..1.1n fQfficti.*l Lih,ali,pn. It asstun, :11.- right to express it•; opinion on circumstances as tht-y aris,..l, and measu-es as they are submitted. Accordin4ly, 0,1,7, is from time to time a cry that the Daily News does not represent Liberal principles—that is to say it does not grind tbe axe of the particular persons or section of party who cry out against it. I suppose not a year passes without some more or less formal resolve to start a new journal that shall be "truly Liberal," that is to say, shall exclusively favour and promote the particular section of Liberalism which at the moment chances to feel itself offended. At the present time such a project is on foot, and has gone so far that a solicitor has issued a circular inviting gentlemen of independent means to entrust him with their money in order to start a new newspaper. In the meantime the Daily News, like the S.Yandard, has just now a larger circulation and a more prosperous business connection than it has bad at any period of its history, and is, moreover, a more powerful factor is political life. From which circumstances it may be pre- sumed that it will go forward on its own way, merely asking to be allowed to manage its own affairs.

It cannot be said that the Art Union of London is not this year—the forty-seventh of its existence—well fulfill- ing the end 7or which it was established. The exhibition, this week, of the pictures and drawings chosen by the prize- winners shows the exercise of considerable taste and judg- ment in the selection. The choice for the most part has been in favour of oil-paintings, and of these the Society of British Artists has come in for the largest share—Mr. "Timber Ships towing to a Berth," and Mr. Hayllar's "The Boit Eyes of the Two," coming from that gallery. From the Royal Academy collection there have been selected "One Generation passeth away and another cometh," by Arthur Stocks; "Harvest Time," by Mr. A. Glendinning; and "Among the Trawiers, Tarbert, Loch Fyne," by Mr. A. Black. The exhibitors at the Albert Hall and the Society of Lady Artists have not been overlooked ; and gqod specimens of the styles of Messrs. James Ma"cCulloch, L. J. Wood, S. P. Jackson, C. Davidson, and T. F. Wainwright are amongst the water-colour drawings that have been honoured by selection. The plate received by every subscriber this year is an engraving of" Stolen by Gipsies," a painting by Mr. Burgess, A.R.A. Next year's plate will be an engraving, by Mr. C. W. Sharpe, of a pic- ture by Mr. Alfred Elmore, entitled the " Tuileries, 20th June, 1792." There were upwards of ten thousand sub- sribers this year.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The wife of a labourer named Lawrence, yesterday, at Reading, drowned her infant three months old in a boiling copper during her husband's absence. She will be brought before the magistrates to-day. Much uneasiness is felt throughout the midland counties by reason of the almost incessant heavy rains which have fallen miring the last fortnight. The fruit crop has suf— fered considerably, much hay still remains ungathered, and the unripe grain in almost every grain growing district has been twaten down by the rain or damaged by the floods. A labourer named John M.Nally was admitted to Bolton Infirmary, on Thursday evening, suffering from severe in- juries to the back of the head, sustained by falling fram the Church of the Saviour, now in course of erection in Pikes Lane. He was in charge of the crane stationed at an eleva- tion of about eighty feet, and he slipped off the scaffolding accidentally. Considerable astonishment was caused in Sheffield, yes- terday morning, by the announcement that Alderman Mountain, Silverdale House, Dore, near Sheffield, had filed a petition in bankruptcy with liabilities amounting to £55,000. Mr. Mountain has been a member of the Corpo- ration some years, and is chairman of the Highway Com- mittee. He has over speculated in land and buildings. An inquest was held at Woolwich, yesterday, upon a girl, aged nineteen, who had committed suicide by poison. It appeared she had received an anonymous threatening letter because she kept company with a specified young man, who was himself led to break off his engagement with her because of aspersions on her character, which were now proved to be unfounded. A verdict of temporary insanity was returned.

AN ILLICIT DISTILLER SELLING DISEASED MEAT.—Yes- terday morning a widow, described as a butcher and milk seller, named Simpson, who only a few months ago was liberated from Stafford Gaol after undergoing a period of imprisonment for being concerned in the illicit manufac- ture of whisky, was sent to gaol by the Hanley magistrates for two months for offering diseased meat for sale in the public market. At IVolverhampton yesterday, Harriet Smith and Sarah Smith, gipsies, were charged with pretending to tell fortunes. The prisoners visited a confectioner's shop where two girls were employed as assistants, and one of them was induced to give the woman two shillings to tell her fortune, which was that she would he married in less than twelve months to a young man, and would have plenty of children. The prisoners were sent to gaol for one month as rogues and vagabonds. ALLEGED EMBEZZLF,MENT RY i TRAVELLER.—CaIeb J. Davies, a commercial traveller, in the employ of Messrs. Hignett, Bros., and Co., tobacco merchants and manufac- turers, of. Liverpool, was yesteTday committed for vial at the s-ssions on a charge of embezzling £5OO, the moneys of his employers. It was stated that the prisoner was in re- ceipt of a salary of £l5O yearly, with £7 per week ex- penses. The defalcations had been going on for a consi- derable time.

IHE REFRIGERATOR Fts..a CARS —The fish experiments 7;rth refrigerator cars for conveying fish fresh to London and other English markets have turned out unfortunate. A break down on Wadnesday caused a delay, and on Thursday afternoon the car had to be detached and left at the Hill- side Station, near Wick, through the heating of the axles by overloading. Four more cars will be despatched to-day. The new system is very popular with fish curers, but over- loading will have to ba prevented in future. CHAR,;E OF STEALING A HORSE AND CAB.—Ye9terd:ty morning, at Burnley, Alfred Hindle, a cabman, was com- mitted for trial on a charge of stealing a horse, cab, gearings, and rugs, value £3O, the property of Thomas A. Hepworth, cab proprietor, Barnley. Last Chtistmas morning the pro- .ecutor's stabla and coach house were broken into, and the horse, atte taken. The prisoner was seen driving the animal through Burnley, and afterwards traced through Blackburn and to Prestott, where the horse was found in a roadside. SHUif FIGHT 11. T ALDERSHOT : VOLUNTEERS C_CNIPLI- MENTED.--A sham 'fiAlat came off yesterday morning on the Fox Hill, Aldershot. About. 3 000 volunteers now in garri- son took part in the proceedings, and acquitted themselves most creditably, their firing and marching being highly commended by the commander-in-chief of the Aldershot forces. Sir A Alison. The idea was that the enemy's ad- vanced guard had reached Basingstoke Canal, and were about to seize the Fox Hill. The battle was prcnouneed

DESTRUCTIVE TIRE AT NORM STlntias.:--Early yester- day morning a tiro of a destructive character occurred at the High Brewery, North Shields, belonging to Messrs. Wm. Henry Allison and Sons. The brewery occupies a large river fron'age, and the brigades of both the river and borough police poured water on the burning premises. the forrder from the floating fire engine and the latter from hydrants on th,i•shore. Despite their efforts, however, the malt house was completely destroyed. The books in the office were removed to a place of safety. The damage which is estimated at £B,OOO is covered by insurance.

div.head: PREMIER.
div.p: THE PREMIER.

A Chester correspondent states that the Premier will leave London immediately after the rec.ss for Hawarden Castle, where he will join Mrs. Gladstone and family, and after- wards probably spend a few d;tys at one of the North Wale:, watering-places. Last year the right hon. gentleman stayed at Penmaenmawr, but this season it is possible that Colwyn Bay will be selected as Mr. %V. H. Gladstone with his wife and family, are already staying there. Mr. Gladstone asQured the correspondent that there is no truth in the state- ment which had gnaw the rounds of the press that Mr. Glad- stone shortly contemplated a visit to his constituents at Midlothian. No arcanzements whatever have ben made to that effect. Mr. Gladstone, however, is in the enjoyment of excellent health, and will doubtless endeavour to fulfil the enjoyment which last year had to be summarily aban. doned in corflsequence of Di-health.

THE MADAGASCAR INCIDENT. RELATIONS BETWEEN ENGLAND AND FRANCE. A Paris telegram of Thuralay night says:—The Tele- graphe, which often receives semi-official communications, asserts that the English Government has not shown itself satisfied with the explanations concerning the Madagascar incident by the French Ambassador in London. The ex- planations were not in accord with the intelligence received by Mr. Gladstone's Cabinet. M. Waddington having counselled M. Challemel-Lacour to make certain concen- sions to British susceptibilities, the French Minister has forwarded fresh and more conciliatory instruction's to M. Waddington. AN ISLE OF MAN BOAT IN COLLISION. EXCHING SCENE ON THE MERSEY. At a few minutes past one o'clock yesterday the Isle of Man Steamer Nlona's Isle ran down a fishing smack just outside the river, and about three miles from New Brighton. Oue man who was in the smack lost his life, notwithstand- Ug the ,rear eff ,rts that were made to save him. The Thma's Is !omeis crowd-cl with passng,rs, and when the collision occurr ii a s.c,ot3 of great excitement took place of, Inert!. Those vibu ..ritncssed the occurrence say that it was

impossible for the "shrimper" to get out of the way, and that the two men in her shouted and whistled in order to attract the attention of those on board the Isle of Man st:.amer, which was coming straight down on her at full speed. By some mischance, however, the men who should have been on the "look out" on board the steamer had failed to notice the little craft, which came into collision with the paddle-box. The fishing smack was smashed into atoms, or, as one of the passengers states, seemed to be "knocked into dust." A boat was instantly lowered from tbe Mona's Isle, and after some little time one of the unfortunate men was picked up. The other poor fellow was not seen at all, and it is supposed that he must have been killed in the fatal crash. The man who was brought on board was very much exhausted, and a collec- tion 'was made for him amongst the passengers, as be lost all he possessed in the boat. The Mona's Isle, strange to say, sustained hardly any damage.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT-
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT-
HOUSE OF LORDS.

The Earl of DUNRAVEN moved the second reading of the Labourers' (Ireland) Bill. After discussioh the motion was agreed to.—Lord BALFOUR, of Burleigh, moved the second reading of the Cruelty to Animals Act Amendment Bill, the object of which was to put down pigeon shooting from traps. He condemned the practice as cruelty that could not pro- perly be called sport.—Earl REDESDALE moved the rejec- tion of the Bill.—Discassion on the Bill was continued by Lord Ribblesdale, Lord Denman, the Duke of Argyle, Earl Wemyss, and Lord Westbury.—Earl GRANVILLE suppm ted the second reading on the grounds of humanity.—Earl FORTESCUE opposed and objected to the time of the House being frittered away when it was required to pass a Bill for the better production of young women and girls —The Bill was rejected by 30 to 17.—The Lord CHANCELLOR moved the second reading of the Bankruptcy Bill.—The Marquis of SALISBURY objected to so unfortunate a Bill being intro- duced so late in the session.—After observations from Earl Fortescue and Lord Fitzgerald, the Bill was read a second time.—The Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Bill was read a third time, and passed.—Adjourned.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

THE PUBLIC PROSECUTOR.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL, replying to Sir G. Campbell, said it was quite true that a departmental committee engaged making inquiry into the office of Public Prosecutor had adjourned without making a report. CRIMINAL APPEAL BILL.—Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Sir Stafford Northcote, declined withdrawing the Criminal Appeal Bill until the House had expressed its opinion on the subject. THE TRAMWAYS AND PUBLIC COMPANIES (IRELAND) BILL.—On the motion for going into committee on the Tramways and Public Companies (Ireland) Bill Mr. BIGGAR objected on the ground that the bill would be of no practi- cal good to Ireland.—Sir E. WfizaoT took a different view, and thought the Government deserved the thanks of the country for introducing the measure.—Mr. HEALY strongly opposed the authority the bill gave grand juries. It armed them with the power of inflicting the whole taxa-

tion. The bill proposed on the unfortunate taxpayers; while it altogether exempted landlords from contributing one penny in relief of the rates. He utterly condemned the emigration classes, and said by emigrating large bodies of Irish people they would not prevent the undying hatred of unfortunates el, iven from home and country. The Government were sowing dragons teeth and he wished them joy of their crop.— Mr. TREVELYAN defended the bill, and said the only object the Government had in bringing it forward was the good of Ireland.—After a long discussion, the House went into committee on the bill.—On clause 1, which gives the power to grand juries to make presentments in favour of the baronial guarantee under the bill, a discussion ensued, and an amendment was moved by Mr. HEALY that the poor- law guardians be substituted for the grand jury.—Mr. TREVELYAN opposed, as the amendment would practically destroy the bill.—The amendment was withdrawn.— Mr. [ALOE moved an amendment to the clause to provide that the grand ju• yl should 'not guarantee payment of dividends beyond four per cent.—Mr. TRk.VELYAN could not accept the amendment. —Mr. HEALY thought it absolutely , necessary some limit should be imposed on the powers of the grand jury.—After discussion it was agreed to insert the words" providing the guarautee should not exceed five per cent," and the amendment was withdrawn.—Colonel NOLAN moved sn addition to the clause giving the right, if deemed advisable, of appeal to the Lord Lieutenant in Council from the decisions of the grand jury when they de- cided against any proposal for tramways.—Tne ATTORNEY- GENERAL for Ireland opposed the proposed addition to the clause.—After discussion the proposal was negatived, and the clause agreed to.—On Clause 2, an amendment by Cap- tain O'SnEA was agreed to, making the number of cess- payers who might appeal to the Lord-Lieutenant against the presentment of the grand jury 20 instead of 6.—The clause was agreed to, as were clauses op to 10 —Clause 11, which provided that the .111111 of £200,000 should be provided for emigrat:on, and that XS instead of £5 ehould be paid each piety emigrating WAS agreed to.—Progress was reporttd, and the sitting suspended.
IMPURF, WATER AT LYMII.

LOCAL BOARD PROSECUTION. Yesterday, at Lynam Petty Sessions, Wm. Ardern, joiner, Lyme), being the owner of premises on which is a well, or spring of water cal led or known by the name of Statham Speut, the water from which is used by man for drink or other domestic purposes, and which is pelluted so as to be iejurious to health, was summoned to show cease why the well should not be closed.—Mr. Ridgway appeared for the Lymtn Local Board, and said that the proceedings were taken under section 70 of the Public Health Act, 1875. He read a portion of the section of the Act, which was to the effect that on the re- port of my person to any locel authority that within their district the water in any well, tank, pump, or cistern, used or likely to be used by man for drinking or other domestic purposes, is so polluted as to be injurious to health, any such authority may apply to '`..t court of jurisdiction to remedy the same, and such court may either dismiss the application or may make an order that such well, tank, pump, or cistern may be closed, or used for certain pur- poses only.—'l'he assist cot magistrates' clerk said that the spout must cotne shin the meaning of the words men- tioned in the sectTsn, viz , well, pump, cistern, or tank, or the magistrates would have no power in the case. Mr. Rdeway said that so far as could be ascertained the spout was only a short length of pipes which conveyed the water a short distance from the well. He must te!l the Bench that a local authority could not go to a man's property and dig a hole to see whether there eves a well or not. The probable cause of pollution in this case was a manure wharf on the erne! bank; and that was another element which was difficult for the Board to deal with in this ease, but to prevent the forming of a manure heap in that district would be a much greater in- kedice than asking their worships to close the spout. Some years ago, before the Lynam Waterworks Company had laid their mains, the spout was used by a great number of people, At the present time, with the exception of any boatmen that might use it. something like seven or eight families were really dependent upon it with a total number of about 30 or 40 persons, while the others who used it had proper supplies in th,ir houses. There was a section of the Public Health Act which gave the Board power to have any manure removed under 24 hours' notice, and the Board exercised that power, but the mere fact of rein falling on the manure wharf caused s traething to percelete through the earth into the well. The matter had been before the Board for a long time—for sev,ral years—And the reason steps hai bee] taken at the present. time was owing to the cholera, and the 14,cel Clover. meet BOW d having issued notices to the locel authorities respectittg i.tiler matters to the one now under consideretiou. ‘Vtiat the Board really asked was that the defendant should take such steps that the public could not get the water. 01 he defendaer, he thought, had rightly come before their worships Airing them to bear the case and decide upon it, for although the well was on private property, it bad been used by the public for a long time, and if the de'endent had fallen in with the Board at the first and closed the well he would have been liable to an action at common law, but the case would be altered if the Bench made an o:der for the well to be closed for the public benefit. The Board only wished the well to be closed for drinking purposes, and they did net wish any costs to fall on the def: ndant, le the application was being made for the good of the district.—Mr. Mort, nuisance inspector for the Board, on being exatnined, said that from what persons told him the water from the spout came from a well, but he did not know himself that it did. He took a sample from the well on the 10th inst. It was not a dry day, but there was no manure in the wharf. at the time. The town's pipes were laid within a very ehort distance of the place, but not- withstanding this the peeple went to the well for water.— Asked by the Bench why people used the water from the well, be said that he did not know unless they liked it Letter. (A Vol& : Because there's more lady in it.) Dr. Fox, medical officer to the Board, staid he repeived a sample of water from Mr. , Mort, on the 1011 instant, anti he bad analysed it. He bad prepared a report, but it only related to organic matter which was the eource of impurity in the water, prejudicial to health, and which had a distinct bearing on cholera, diarrhoee, and typhoid. The sample contained 108 grains of chlorine per gallon, free ammonia 0-40 parts per mil- lion, and alburninoid 0.16: The water was polluted by sewage matter, aed if that sewage matter contained any elements of tbe swcific diseases he had mentioned, all par- takers of the water would become victims to the complaint. The erdinary senses of the people should tell them that the water was impure, is it was discoloured and had an unplea- sant smell. He found that it was dangerous to allow water th it was not used for drinking purposes to be used for slopping because some persons preferred to use it for drinking Par- p.,ses, either from igeorance or some other reason. He instanced a pump to which hundreds of people in London had sent for water, although it was miles away, and that eimply because the water was bright and sparkling. That weer had been the cause of spreading cholera ever a very wide area. Boiling the water would make it wholesome se far as organic matter was concerned.—The Bench seid they would I be to know whether the spout was a wed, tank, or what it e as, end the c 'se would th'erefote be ad- journed to Peat reeesiorte in order tilAt this :night be ascer- tained.

div.head: RUNCORN PUBLIC HALL.
div.p: RUNCORN PUBLIC HALL.

For the past six weeks Runcorn Public Hall has been in the hands of the painter and decorator. During that period the interior has undergone a complete metamorphosis, and those who saw it in the winter months will scarcely recog- nise it as the same building. The once sooty wane and ceiling, and the dingy woodwolif are now resplendent in paint of varied but harmonious colours. laid on with artis-ie taste, and the tout ensemble is exceedingly effective and pretty. The style of decoration followed is the early Eng- lish Conventional, with a slight mingling of Mexican, and has been most elaborlitely carried out. The eeiline divided into p.euele is painted sisy blue in the centre, while the side panels are pale buff ornamented with a seven-inch band of a dark colour. The walls are a light bath stone colour relieved with a nine-inch ornamental bard A deep dado of Indian red runs round the building under the gallery. The wall above the platform is most elaborately decarated, and the columns on each side are painted in panels of effective design, the scroll worked capitals bein4 relieved with gold. The panels in front of the platform aro embellished in unique style, and the woodwork throughout is painted a rich dark colour, the bevelled edges having a coating of Indian red. The platform, with a new crimson curtain supplied by Mr. Francis Fairhurst, as part of the background, presents a charming appearance to the view, and it has excited the admiration of all the persons who have seen it. The coronas are also coloured Indian red, re- lieved with vermilion and buff. The main entrance hall is elegantly decorated. The "small hall "is a miniature copy to some extent of the large room, and the dressing rooms, * eirc., are papered and painted in a most pleasing manner. The directors have taken ad- vantage of the decorative operations to fix a complete system of ventilating apparatus, which was cer- tainly much required, and meetings and conc.rts can t 07v be attended with a greater degree of comfort than formerly. The painting and decoratirg has teen carried out by contract by Mr. George Yarwood, of Church.street. . Runcorn. who is deserving of every praise for the manner in which he has accomplished his work. This has been of • no mean magnitude. The building is very lofty, and an immense scaffold had to be erected. This was successfully done by Mr. Henry White, contractor, of Runcorn, bud it is gratifying to know tbat*not the slightest accident has oc- curred. The hall will be re-opened to-morrow (Sunday), when the anniversary services of the Runcorn Branch of the Mersey Missions to Seamen will be held. W. P. Roberts, Esq., of Liverpool, is announced to deliver ad- dresses, and that gentleman and his wife, who are both well known as admirable singers of sacred melodies, will sing a few solos. Crowded congregations are expected, and admission is by ticket only.

div.head: ROBBING PETER TO
div.p: ROBBING PETER TO
PAY PAUL.
BY JOHN SAUNDERS. Author of HIRELL ; OR, LOVE BORN OF STRIFE." "ABEL DR IKE'S WIFE," "ISRAEL MORT, OVERMAN," &C., &C.

CHAPTER I.—A NOVELTY IN MARCH DAYS. The winter of the year 18— was a most unconscionable one; taking possession as it did of a great part of Autumn on the one side, and of Spring on the other, and threatening the entire extinction of tho latter, so far as the passing

• season was conc3rned. But March Came, and wonderful indeed was the charge be wrought in a day or two. One might liken him to a Florist to whom the Heavenly Gardener had confided the care of the flowers of the earth, in preparation for some august holiday; who had in consequence gathered them together, and sedulously protected them, in order to take the time of east winds .by day, and of black frosts by night, to pour them forth amid balmy breezes Upon the . world, while he stood by to see, as Chaucer says : " How all the Orient laugheth of the sight!" Men who rarely ever spoke to each other stopped quite naturally to exchange congratulations in the London streets, sometimes under the shelter of umbrellas provided against the sleet and wind rather than in fear of rain. Dreary, blackened hedgErows became suddenly alive with tiny sparkling leaf buds, which rushed out at the call of the sun like so many children in a squalid neighbourhood, crowding forth when the inspiring streams of music are heard frpm passing holiday-makers, inviting all to follow

their example. Flowers sprang us by magic in every suburban garden. 1 The hoarse cries uf the kiwker, "all a growing and a blow- I ing," was heard alike in well-to-do quarters, tempting buyera to his fall baskets of lovely but tender blossoms (forced into rapid bloom to decay as quickly), and in the veriest back slums to which he or she carried violets or primroses. Surely there is here one of the most pathetic of combinations. The bringer and the people to whom they are brought, in all their dirt, and rags, and homeless homes, and coarseness et face, word and gesture on one hand, and the flower,' on the other, so pure, bright, fresh, fragrant, full of the very breath of heaven, and yet taken by the pariahs of our State, in admiratien, sympathy, and love, that are unable to express themselves except through grotesque forms, but are not the less true and intrinsically beautiful. If we may indeed thank God for flowers on our own ac- count, still more should we thank Him in our heart of hearts for the blessings they bring to the poor, the ignorant and the depraved. CHAPTER 11.--HARLAXTON HOUSE, MAYFAIR.

No greater contrast to the homes just glanced at, or to the flowers which alone suit the tastes and pockets of their inmates, could well be presented than by Harlaxton House, and its adornments :on one of those same lovely March days. Amid the formidable and ever-increasing piles and ranges of dwelling-Muses deyoted in our overgrown Metropolis to the use of the nobility, gentry, and commercial magnates who may be roughly said to constitute the fashionable world—dwellings splendid in aspect and cost, but common- place for the most part in their splendour, it is refreshing to come upon some old residence of an aristocratic family; ' rich within, in the gathered art-wealth of centuries; but dull, possibly dingy, without, as seen over the walled-in court yard ; the whole saying so plainly to the showy par- venu erections crowding around; "Pray, good people, keep your distance." i Harlaxton House is a residence of this kind; as uninvit- ing outside as the home of many a Turkish Pasha; but so full within of all that the heart of man or woman can de- sire in comfort, luxury, and picturesque beauty of detail, that the greatest of Eastern potentates might well envy the fortunate possessors; even if he see that the harem at pre- sent consists only of an aged and widowed Countess, and a young girl, an orphaned relative and heiress, who has come to reside with her and her two sons since the death of the late earl, her husband, little more than a year ago. The day on which our story opens has been anticipated as a memorable one in the family. The Countess, and the Earl, her eldest son, give now their first formal dinner party since the loss of their relative, to a few intimate friends; and hold a reception afterwards of the most brilliant cha- racter, considering the titular, political, and intellectual rank of those who have been invited, and among whom is a Prince of the Royal blood. Most of these anticipate with interest and sympathy the return to the fashionable fold of one conspicuous in for- mer days as a leader of society ; and esteemed in later ones for her kindness to young aspirants of either sex, an for her willingness to aid by purse and pen in any good work. A long waggon stands before the outer gate filled with plants; the taller ones nodding to each ether at every movement of the soft breeze, as if whispering about the glory of the day which invests foliage and flowers with golden sheen. Here the eye rests on slender palms in oriental beauty of form ; red-le ived and variegated dracaenas splendid in colour-foliage ; and accacias studded all over with tiny golden buttons of blooira-;—while there it is attracted by the arching and broadly waving fronds of a giant tree-fern, which overtopl bushy camellias in full flower—red, white, striped, and rose-hued. The florist's men are busy unloading, and have to throw off their cats, tuiti put forth all their strength to lift some of the heavy weights, and carry them through the court- yard into the ball. This presents a busy scene. Immense numbers of smaller plants, of the kinds most distinguished for beauty of leaf and blossom (the large and lovely snow-white, vase-shaped flowers of the Calla X:hiopica, gleaming n herever one looks), are close packed against the sombre, armour-clad walls; waiting till their larger brethren shall be first dis- posed of in pride of place in the decoration of the hall and staircase, the saloon, and other apartments. Servants in the elegant blue livery of the Harlaxtons are passing to and fro on the business of the evening; while two of their number, in waiting, stand idly gazing and gossiping with each other, in luxurious enjoyment of the bustle and activity all around, since they are not called upon to partake. So they think. But vain are the hopes of man! Two of the florist's men, who have just come in, and are stagger- ing under the burden of a grand palm, find it so task their strength, that one of them cries out, suddenly— "l say, Bill, I must let go, if you don't stop." "Easy, then!" responds the other, and they manage to let it gently down. Aware that time presses, theyirk round for help; and lo! the two lackeys. "Lend a hand; there's good fellows," says one of the men to the nearest servant; "it's more than we can man- age." The person addressed came, looked at the plant, looked at the two men, went slowly back to his comrade, said some- thing to him, then both looked back and laughed. "There's a man and a hrother for you!" exclaimed the florist's man who had made the appeal. "You a man and brother of a gorgush creature like that!" said the other. "I'm ashamed on you, Jem, so to mistake your proper spere. Why, he's a sort o' human bird o' paradise." The lackeys heard, and again they laughed. "Now, I look again," remarked the previous speaker, "he gives me the idear of a splendid tuelip as nil fall to pieces at the first puff of wind. Only look at his legs ?" The legs so commented on changed their position uncom- fortably, the face of their owner reddened with anger, and he turned as if not to hear. But this only made the next speaker raise his voice accordingly: "And his complexion! Not long for this world, Bill !" "Think so? Then don't aggrevate his feelings mean- while. Let us hope he may live long, and make the werry rainbows fade afore him!" It was too much. The lackeys advanced threateningly, and the florist's men, with a laugh, confronted them with folded arms. yirhether that silently insulting attitude would have provoked the servants to show their manhood, who shall say ?.. for they lost or were spared the oppor- tunity through the entrance of a respectable-looking man in black—Mr. Richards, the house steward, and master of the domestics. The first glimpse of him sent them both 1 back with extraordinary rapidity, and at the same time changed their attitude; in an equally remarkable manner they became conspicuously busy. "Are all the plants in from the court-yard?" he asted. He was answered in the affirmative. "Then hurry with them to their places. I expect the Countess here in a few minutes on a tour of inspection to see that all is right." There was a large plant near where he stood. He called the florist's men to take it to a place in the hall, which he indicated to them. Then noticing the plant which had been the occasion for the recent quarrel, he told the two servants to take that to another part. They hesitated, looked at the florist's men,—who put their hands to their backs in an ironically sympathetic way,—and seemed half inclined to refuse; but Richards' stern— • "What are you dawdling about ?" was decisive. With great difficulty they lifted, and bare the plant to its place. But even that was not so hard to bear as the jeers and con- gratulations of the florist's men, when for a nument they had to pass near them.
CHAPTER 111.-A PASSING GLIMPSE OF OUR CHIEF CHARACTERS.

A GOLBORNE INNKEEPER FINED FOR SELLING ADUL- TERATED WHIsKEY.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Thomas Hirst, landlord of the Queen Anne, Gol- borne, was summoned for selling whiskey adulterated with water to an extent more than that allowed by the law.— The defendant pleaded guilty.—Superintendent Weir said that on the 28th June -he visited the defendant's house and purchased a pint of Irish whisky, for which be paid 2s. He afterwards sent a sample to the public analyst at Liverpool, who had since certified that it was 331. per cent. under proof —l4 per cent. more than the utmost limit allowed by law. —Detendant was fined 20s. and costs. Mr. Moore appeared for the,complainant.—The evi- dence showed that a quarrel had taken place between the parties, during which the defendant canee oat with a poker and shovel and "panned" them near the complainant's face. —The case was dismissed.—Thomas Bradburn (for whom Mr. Moore appeared) was summoned for assaulting Wil- liam Henry Allen, a lad, on the 6.h inst. The defendant is one of the managers at Mitchell's Paper Works, and the complainant was employed under him. It was alleged that the defendant "boxed" defendant's ears to such an extent that they bled.—The cross-examination of 9ne of the wit- nesses by Mr. Moore elicited the fact that the complainant kept crying out "Hallelujah" and "Praise the Lord" in order to vex the defendant, who was a Primitive Methodist. —For the defence it was maintained that the lad had not done his work, and had, in addition, been very impudent. The defendant simply "corrected" him in a proper manner. —The case was dismissed. GOLBORNE CATHOLIC SCHOOL TREAT.—The annual treat to the scholars attending the Golhorne Catholic School took place on Saturday afternoon last, in favourable weather. A petite, number of "old scholars" attended to take part in the joyous gathering, and with friends and members of the congregation nearly 1,500 persons walked in a procession through the town. The scholars and friends assembled at the church about a quarter-past two, and after a short ser- vice therein, conducted by the new priest, the Rev. Father Byrne (who also addressed a few wise counsels to the scholars), the procession was formed. Headed by the band of the St. George's Industrial School (Liverpool), the prin- cipal streets of the town were paraded. Large numbers of persons assembled to witness the imposing demonstration. Special selections were played by the band near the resi- dences of Mr. Unsworth and Mr. i3rewis. On arriving back at the school the annual tea meeting was held, the room being twice densely filled with those who partook of the good things provided. After tea the scholars adjourned to a field, kindly lent by Mr. Uneworth, where the usual games and festivities were indulged in until dusk put a stop to the proceedings. Everyone appeared to have spent a very pleasant and enjoyable afternoon. WATCH •ROBEERIES AT GOLBORNE.—Considerable talk has been occasioned in Golborne by the recent theft of several watches under circumstances of a singularcharacter. One day last week a young man went to the house of a newly-married couple, not far from the police station, and asked if he might stay there for the night. As he was well-known to the couple—being a near relative—they allowed him to do so, and found him a bed. Ointhe follow- ing morning the husband went to his work as usael, leaving his wife in bed. When the latter came downstairs, she ascertained that the "ledger" had disappeared without even bidding her good-bye, or thanking her for the kindness shown to him. Shortly afterwards two watches, a hat, a ' shawl, dm., could not be found, and the only conclusion to be arrived at was that the " relative-lodger" had decamped with them. He has aince been at liberty, although efforts have been. made to discover his whereabouts. Another robbery, more daring than the one just narrated, occurred on Saturday fore- noon last. A man called at a house near the stores of the Leigh Co-operative Society and asked for lodgings. He in- duced a female in the house to go up the stairs on some pre- text or other, and when she came down she- found that the inquirer for lodgings had not waned untilshe returned, but had left the house and taken with him a wotoh, value seven guineas. The police were immediately. informed of the robbery, and a description of the thief was given to them,but up to the present they have failed to apprehend him. It is stated that the same fellow had previously asked at another house in the neighbourhopd for a loan of 10s. while he fetched his luggage from tha station. It is almost needless to add that the money was not forthcoming, and that the story of his "luggage at the station" was a mere invention. , ARREST OF A DESERTER AT ST. Hlimues.—tut the St. HAYDOCK. , R A.INEIILL. PARISI! Cimnani—Special sermons were preached in the Parish Church, Bainhill, on Sunday, by the Rev. A. S. Maclean, vicar of St. John's, Longton, Staffordshire,. and formerly of St. Helens. There was a large congregation at each service and the collections, which were made towards defraying the expenses recently incurred in cleaning and decorating the church, were liberal. SUDDEN DEATH.—Margaret Perry, wife of William Perry, , St. Helens-road, Rainbill, died suddenly on Wednetalay morning. She had been ailing for some time, and about half-past ten on Wednesday morning she mentioned to one of her neighbours that she felt worse, and went to bed. A few minutes afterwards she died. Dr. Packer was called in, but was unable to certify the cause of death. WIGAN. leViiinGrofjutlNieCTplrOoNprßieltOirLsWoAf?thiCs°rl'aiirlwA,Nay r.—Tlwas day in the boardroom of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lin- colnshire Rail way Company, Manchester, Mr. N. Eckersley, re fn -yTe aurels mey - the chairman, presiding. The Chairman moved the adop- tion of the report and statement of accounts. The report was as follows:—" The whole of the heavy ,aork on the main line has now been tinished,and the permanent way laid down. With the exception of the temporary station at Darlington-street, Wigan, which is well in hand, the plat- forms for all stations on the line have been constructed, and the station buildings and goods warehouses are now rapidly approaching completion. It is anticipated that the line will be ready to be opened for passenger and goods traffic early in November. In the past session of Parliament the Man- chester, Sheffield and Lincolshire Company have obtained powers for an extension of this company's line through Wigan to a junction with the West Lancashire Railway, near Preston. which, besides affording the means of con- structing a Central Station in Wigan will, it is hoped, be a valuable feeder to the company's railway. The directors regret very much to announce the death of their colleague, James Burrows, who has been a director of the company from its commencement, and to whom the directors have been much indebted for valuable advice and assistance." Mr. R. Darlington seconded the resolution, which was passed.—There was no other business before the meeting.
THE DEATH IN A CIRCUS AT ST. HELENS.

On Friday last an inquest was held by Mr. Coroner Barker, at St. Helens, touching the death of the boy James Harrison, 12 years of age, who lived at 48, Lord-street, Gerard's Bridge, and was killed on the previous Wednesday evening whilst attempting to ride a mule in Culeen's Cir- cus, St. Helens. It appeared that it had been the custom at this circus in the course of the evening performances to invite boys from among the audience to attempt to ride a inule which was trained to "throw" them if possible. Hitherto nothing but diversion has resulted from this operation. On the night in question the deceased accepted the invitation, but was as usual thrown and was seen to stagger to the barrier in front of the reserved seats, and shortly after he expired. A lad named John Magin said that he saw the deceased thrown twice, and on attempting to mount a third time be saw the mule kick him some- where in the stomach and then he staggered to the barrier. Another youth named Gregory said he saw the deceased stagger and put his hand on his chest, but did not see the mule kick him Mr. Culeen, the proprietor of the circus, said he had had the mule about 12 months, and it was trained to throw people off by putting its head to the floor and kicking up its hind legs. It was net shod with iron. He was himself working the animal on the night of the occurrence and was positive it did not kick the deceased.—Dr. Jamison spoke to having examined the body of the deceased and was of opinion that death had been caused by a form 1 appoplexy brought on by over-excitement. He was perfectly sure that death was not the result of a kick or other Violence.—A verdict oi "Death from natural causes " was returned, death in tho opinion of the jury probably being caused by a fusion on the brain brought on by excitement. Some of the larymen thought the public ought not to be invited to ride the mule, but the Coroner pointed out that as the jury had not , attached blame to anyone they could not make a formal Ipreaentment, but must leave it to Mr. Culeen's considera- tion. Mr. Culeen, he supposed, had to cater for the public, land the public were never satisfied unless something extra- ordinary was being done. He was quite sure Mr. Culeen would do his best to protect the public, but, if they would he dangerous things done, he thought the public more to blame than the proprietors.
