div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The Finance Committee ;;;;-in-inended the following ac- clunts to be paid :—Water Committee, £279 is 7d ; Gas, £393 12s 91; Highway, £B7 4s 4d; Hospital, £8 15s; Health, £B5 103 6d; Market, £7 18s; Sewerage, £246 35 sd; Finance, £2,310 143 id.—A rough sketch of the pro- posed public offices was submitted, and consideration was deferred.—On the motion of Mr. WRIGHT, seconded by Mr. SADLER, the minutes were passed.

_ . THE MIDWOOD-HERSHAW BREACH. Mr. KERSHAW then rose to speak on the motions of which he had given notice, expressing the hope that the matter would be conducted in a fair spirit. The first motion was that the resolution ordering sett crossings to be laid down in Travis, Midwood, and 01tier-streets be rescinded. Although he had given this notice the work had been done, and he held, that the Board would not order the crossings to be taken up agair. Under the circumstances he thought it would not be wise for him to proceed further, but he thought it was the duty of the Highway Committee to have left the work in abeyance antil his motion had been consi- dered. The committee had, according to the bye-laws, done wrong in making the crossings, because they ought to be ' put in at the owners' expeuse.—Mr. MutwoOD : We don't ask him to withdraw, Mr. Chairman. We are prepared to defend our action.—Mr. KERSHAW said he was bound to withdraw in face of 'chat had happened. He did not wish to move a vote of censure, but was rather anxious to help on everything amicably. He did think, however, that the , Board ought to express the opinion that the Highway I Committee should have allowed the work to remain in abey- ance. Ile committee had exceeded their duty in proceed- ing with this work when he had given notice to rescind. He then withdraw that motion; and referring te the one he had put on the paper, to rescind the resolution approving of; the digging in front of Messrs. Handley and Beck's shop, he said his reaeon for this course was that he might ask Mr. Midwood to substantiate the charges he made againet him at the last meeting. He thanked Mr. Dutton for his action on that occasion, but was afraid the work it approved would be made a precedent on future occasions, and pointed out that a resolution was passed in 1882 that the surveyor do no work without the sanction of the com- mittee and Board. Instead of moving the rescinding of Mr. Dutton's motion, be would move that the Board disap- prove of the work being done without the sanction of the Highwiy Committee an 1 Board.—Mr. MIDWOoD : Are we not wasting our time? How can he move such a thing without he gives notice P—The Chairman answered in the negative.—Mr. KERSHAW said he wanted Mr. Midwood to substantiate his charges.— Ile CHAIRMAN' : The que,tion .is not before the Board, inasmuch as you have withdrawn the request.—Mr. KERSHAW denied this, adding that he had given Mr. Midwood private notice.—Mr.DIIITON : Can a private member mak) a statement and then sit down with- out making a motion ?—The CHAIRMAN : He has with- drawn the motion, and is allowed to make an explanation. . 1. :1141. ext.)llßAti... I.- k...., ~.—.........:--t : ~. „. which will be duly reported, and no answer at present will Ibe permitted. That seems to ins to be hardly fair without ,he ends with a onotion.—Mr. MIDWOOD : That's it. It is not fair.—The CHAIRMAN thought it would only be fair for Mr. Midwood to make an explanation.—Mr. KERSHAW : To the charges I—Mr. MIDwOOO : lam willing to do that. I should like to knew from Mr. Kershaw where 1 must com- mence? He has given me so many notices, Mr. Chairman, I don't kuow where to begin.—Mr. KERSHAW slid he called upon Mr. Midwood to prove the alle- gations he made at the special meeting: let, that he ordered the sewer to be put in his yard; 2111, that he ordered the surveyor to sewer his property in Deacon-road; 3rd, with draining his new shops in Victoria-road, and the kerbing done in Millfield-lane. The allegation was that these were done by the surveyor at the Board's cost.—Mr. WEBiTER seconded the motion to give an opportunity for reply.—Mr. Mil:moon said his explanation would simply be a repetition of his statements at the last meeting, and read letters and extracts from the minutes as the foundation for his charges. The draining of Mr. Kershaw's property was done by the Board free of cost, Mr. Kershaw contended, because then property owners had not paid. That state- ment was not correct, for all the individuals who had Work done in the same road paid for it, and Mr. Webster was one of the number. (Laughter.)—Mr. WEBSTER: You are mistaken there. He afterwards admitted that he had paid for sewering done in Widnes-road.—Mr. MIDWOOD then re- iterated the charges he made at the last meeting, concluding by the remark that he had defended the Highway Coita- -1 mittee as far as they needed, and declined to take the matter further.—Mr. KERSHAW, in reply, asked the mem- bers to put away any prejudiced feeling between Mr. Mid- wood and himself, and proceeded to deal with the charge respecting his timber yard. He read letters dated in 1873, in which he claimed toe right to drain into the Hntchinsou-street sewer, which, however, was not

at that time fully laid. The Board did not take the matter any further, although he offered to pay a portion of the ex- pense of bringing the sewer up, and in 18M, when there was two or three feet of water in the cellars of two of his houses in Hutchinson-street, he again wrote to the Board. But his friend stated that he got the drains put in while chairmen of the committee. (Mr. MIDWOOD: He was. He gave this a direct negative. Let Mr. Mid wood prove that be told the surveyor to do the work. With regard to Victoria-road, he contended that the drain was brought to Greenall's puAichouse at the end of Alexandria-street, and all they had to do was to carry it from there to his houses. He made applic)tion to the Board for the drain to be taken and if the Board saw fit to do the thing he was not to blame. He was not a number at that tinr..t. He denied that the

surveyor brought the drain to his property in Deacon-road. He knew he brought it somewhere, he did not know where. He appeared before tha Highway Committee and ask,-;d them, "If you don't charge otlyrs why charg,l. rue ? " The surveyor repli, d that he (Mr. Kershaw) had always bean hard against him, and he thought, he ought to be hard against him, and that he ought to be charged if no one else was. The Financa Committee knocked the charge off. Therefore there was no blame att tolling to him (Mr. Ker- shaw) there. The kerbing in Millfield-lane was done with the authority of the committee if not the Board, in consider- ation of a strip of land which he and Mr. Glover gave al mg the road. He concluded : I think, sir, that these allegations made by my friend could not be true. I my- self should blush to remain here as a member of this Board, if I used my office simply to further my own (amis. I should never think of entering this room any more, and I deny that my conduct ever has been such while a member of this Bo trd.—The CHAIRMAN remarked upon the amity and harmony which had characterised the discussion, and hoped it would go no further. MR. WEBSTER POSES AS AN ECONOIIT.S7.—IMP,RTAN

div.head: DISCUSSION.
div.p: DISCUSSION.

/ Mr. WEISTER moved that the Board take into considera- tion the appointment of a law cl•eic. The Boatd knew what had taken place at Bootle, and what they were doing in the matter. The advice of a law clerk would be very useful, and there would be a saving of time and railway expenses if one were appointed. It would be cheaper to have a law clerk even if they had to do same as Bootle Loci! Board and pay a salary of SYS). ("No, no.")—Mr. WRIGHT sail Mr. Webster's explanation of his motion was not sufficient. —Mr. WEBSTER : It's sufficient for you.—Mi. SADLER: As Mr. Webster is trying to pose as the economist of the Board and attempts to make it seem as if other members are doing nothing in the matter I will second the motion in order to bring it before the Board without pledging myself Ito vote for it.—Mr. Durrort was sure every member would endeavour to exercise the greatest prudence in their coun- cils, the greatest humility in their thoughts, and the very best charity in their words, and as this motion affected their relation with the highest official of the Board, he , thought it ought to be discussed in committee. He moved I that the Board consider the question in committee. Mr Minwoop said if the mover of the resolution knew as much of the working of the Board as he (Mr. Mid wood) did, he would never go in for a law clerk. Mr. Webster had not gone the right war' about it ever to change his (Mr. Mid- wood's) views. 1,;o gentleman who rose at that Board in a fury, and said "BO and so," would ever get him to rush into

div.head: TUE EXAMINER. SATITTII)AY, AUGUST 18. 1882.
div.p: TUE EXAMINER. SATITTII)AY, AUGUST 18. 1882.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday, when there Were preset Dr. o'Keetle, Messrs. T. Handley, D. Forster, Wright; Midwood, B. Dutton, J. Houghton, :Caley, Web- ster, Sadler, Kershaw, Allen (clerk), Higginson (surveyor), Carr (gas engineer), Dixon (nuisance inspector). Mr. H.and- ley was voted to the chair, but Mr. Midwood did not think it was advisable for him to take that position, as he might be interested in some discusEion that might take place. Mr. Forster and several other gentlemen were proposed, but de- clined, and ultira del', Dr. O'Keeffe was unanimously elected

ti the chair. THE CONTRACTOR AND THE BOARD. The CLERK read the following letter —"3,: Beach Ter- race, West Bank, Widnes. July 16, IS3.—T) the Widnes Local Board. Grantlemen,—Re sewage works contract No 1. I must at once draw your attention to this contract and to the manner in which I am treated by you and your en- gineer, Mr. Copeland. lam wishful to do all in my power to carry out my contract according to the terms of the spec- fication, titc. Tills I fled is utterly impossible. In the first instance the amount of money paid for the work already executed is a miserable iestal- mut compared to the value of the work 41933. The plans are not fortlrcoming for the work yet to be executed after so many repeated applications. Also work is sought to be imposed a pan me without extra remunera- tion, and no regard is being paid either to the plans or speclacations. As it is impossible for me to carry out the c3atract under the terms sought to b 3 imposed upon.me, I have written to Mr. Higginson, asking him to meet my engineer in order that they may go over all points in dis- pu•.e. In the event of his refusing to do so I shall be under the pateful necessity of referring the matter to my legal ade ser. I will name him on receipt of year answer to this letter if r,quired.—l am, yours truly, ROBERT JEFFREYS, per E. L. W."--The coma-rani:Wien was referred to the ,vr.q,e Committee. SOUTHPORT roRESTIORE.

The following Wl9 read :—'• 10, Downing-3reet, White- hall, July 16. b. 1883. Sir,—l am directed by Mr. Glad- to inform you that he !us rL,ceived the comtnunicatien fr)m tho Widnes Local Board on the subject of the South- port foreshore which you have done him the honour to for- ward to him. 6s. 4d., D. Hirst £7,195 4e. 10d., G G. Rayner .0,955 83 B,l.—Tne minutes were pissed, on the motion of Mr. MID WOOD, seconded by Mr. WEBSTER. lIEALTH COMMITTEE; OUTBREAK OF SMALL PDX. The Medical Officer reported to the Health Committee a case of small pox at No. 20, John-street, off Widnesqoad Four adults and five children were living in the house, the youngest child not being vaccinated, but this had since been done. The patient had been isolated, and was doing well under the charge of Dr. McDonnell. During July there were 97 births and 31 deaths, being at the rate of 46.5 per 1,000 and 14 83 per 1,000 respectively. Zymotic diseases caused three deaths. Referring to cholera, the medical officer said the two dangers against which they must guard were impure water and impure air, and for this purpose he would recomme ed the following measures:- 1. Immediate removal of all accumulations of house refuse an other filth. 2. Examination of water supply where , opal' to suspicion. 3. Keeping the drains pure by means of the free use of chloride of lime. 4. Thorough washing and lime-washing of uncleanly premises, especially lodging-houses. The comatratee gave instructions to ask Mr. Carlile to drain !regnant water in Brictfield, Albert-road, and Mr. Midwood was givee twice that the nu;s trice from flooded cellars in Mid woe,-street must be abated. Regulations received from the Local Government Board re cholera, nrging the neces- sity of being prepared with a hospital into which patients arriving by vessels could be at once removed. Mr. Biddle, of the Lon ion and Notth-Western Railway Compluy, re- fused to let a hoese for the purpose, and instructions were given to inquire about other houses which might be suitable. Illurcenroel moved the passing of the minntee.—rhe CRA.IRMtN seconded, and observed that stagnant water in , cellars was a great source of disease, and they ought to guard against it. The corn nittee hail issued their instruc- tions to dr. Carlil3 in a nada 111 inner to give him an pp- portunity of doing the work. Referring to an infeclous diseases hospital, he said at Weines they were in a miserable state for want of one. There were a few cases of smale pox in the township. and this disease was nearly as bad as cholera, but not qeite so frightful nor decim its the popula- tion to so great an extent as cholera, nor as smallpox used to do in ancient times b3fere vaccination was introduced. Three fresh cases of smallpox had broken out, and the committee had been trying to get places to isolate them near the arches at West B ink, but the landlord refused their offer. The Board might get orders at any moment from the Local Government Board to erect an infectious diseases hospital, and he thought it was incumbent upon the Board to consider what should be done—whether or not to build a hospital in a suitable place at the least possible cost. He did not think that the ratepayers would cry out against an expenditure of money in a matter where their healths were concerned.—No further discussion took place, and the minutes were passed.

an idea of his. (Hear, hear.) The finances of the Board were never in a better state than they were at present, and he attributed this to the management of the Board's present clerk. (Hear, hear.) If Mr. Webster had sat at that Board as he had done, hour after hour trying to make arrangements with the law clerk, he would never have thought of such a motion. The Board was formed in 1865, and up to the present time had paid £20,000 for kw. That was the result of having a law clerk and alen paying a clerk a large salary at the same time. At the end of the year when the Board thought everything was clear there was a bill of extras something like £l,lOO brought in, and in 1879 when they had a law clerk, the arrears of the Board were £20,000. At the present moment they were about £1,200. He, therefore, asked whether they had amended their position since they had a law clerk or not. In 1882 if they had had a law clerk the commissions on loans would have cost £533, and in 1883 £223. It must be patent to everyone that they had only to engage a law clerk and he would make the bill out.—Mr. WRIGHT moved, and air. He had heard Mr. Beasley say the Board must nat do so and so, and he had been teld to shut his mouth aid say nothing abeut it. He (Mr. Kershaw) did net think it rieht that a . profssional men should have these charges brought against him now.—Mr. MIDWOOD said he had made charges ag tinst no- body, and ha should not sit there to hear Mr. Kershaw make such statements.—Mr. KERSHAW did net think it wise to be without a law clerk.—Mr. HANDLEY said the law expenses for the carrent year would not be £lOO, while in former years when there was a law clerk they Amounted to £7OO and £l,OOO a year.—The motion was lost by nine votes to one, only Mr. -Webster votin; for it.— Mr. WEBiTER then moved a reduction of £5O in the salary of Mr. Copeland, the resident engineer. He said the sewer- ae work was proceeding very unsatisfactorily. Mr. Cope- land had no power over the contractor, and was receiving too much money for the work he was doing. During the p Ist minth Mr. Jeff.-evs had done £2lO worth of work, ard the Board had p aid £27 for watching it done, or 13 per cent. If the Board had a privets engineer over the work it might have cast 3or 4 per cent. If the work went on no qaicker it would be time for something to be done, either with the engineer or the centractor.—The motion was not seconded, and therefore fell to the ground.—Mr. WEBSTER prepesed that Mr. Allen's (the clerk's) salary be reduced £lOO per annum. Some time ago the members of the late Beard thonght it wise to advance Mr. Allen's salary £lOO. lie cauld not see what they could see in giving Mr Allen £lOO, when he was going to do no more work, work no more hours than he did before. Therefore he moved that his salary be reduced £loo.—Mr. Durrorr : I think this is out- rageous to the officer, Cannot we speak P—Mr. SADLER No; your mouth is closed.—The motion not being seconded, fell to the ground. RUNCORN COUNFY COURT. TUESD&Y.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkgs, Judge.
There were 47 original plaints and 2 judgment summonses for hearing.
THE RUNCORN FREE CHURCH ACCIDENT.
CLAIM AGAINS' MR. STATHAM.

William Frodsham, paiater and decorator, carrying on business in Lord-street, claimed from William Stetham, contractor and builder, Runcorn, the sum of £5O damages for personal injuries sustained owing to the fall of a scaffold agreed to be erected by the defendant for the plaintiff in a proper manner, and which said scaffold was improperly and negligently constructed and with improper materials, in breach of the !Aid agreement and of the rights of the plaintiff.—Mr. Burton, of Runcorn, appeared for the plain- tiff, and the defendant was represented by Mr. A. Fletcher, of Northwich. A jury, of which Mr. A. Timmis Wee fore- man, was empannelled to hear the case, and in addressing them Mr. Burton stated that in April last the defendant re- quested the plaintiff to give him an estimate for whitening the ceiling of the Methodist Free Church, in Ellesmere-st. He did so, and contracted to do the work for 305., provided the defendaeat would erect the scaffold. Defendant agreed to do so. On the 26,h the defendant informed the plaintiff that the scaffold was ready, and about ten o'clock next morn- ing the plaintiff and his two men went to the place and mouated the sceff ic! to see if it was safe and high enough. One of the men called out that that was not the way- to test the scaff Ad when the defendant, who was present, said it was safe enough, and would carry six men like himself. He had fixed more scaffolds than the plaintiff's men had ever seen. Accordingly the plaintiff, two men, and two appren- tices went on with the work. When they had been at work perhaps an hour, the scaffolding near the pulpit gave way, and the plaintiff fell to the floor and two of his men lodged in the pulpit. The latter not having so far to fall were un- injured, but it was found that the plaintiff had sustained serao is injuries. 'lke muscles of the neck, and the spine of toe back were much injured, and there were unmistakeable symptoms of concussion of the brain. There had been a doctor in attendance upon him ever since At the ends the scaffold was constructed of spars or scantling,much tee weak f at- the purpose. Across these spars were placed scitlllings and rough spars, instead of poles, and upon these were laid the plaintiff's planks. The plaintiff had carried on business in Runcorn four years, and he had been able to obtain an extensive connection. At this time last eye.... h. pioying six men, oaa eine. tee eeektent his business had been at a standstill. As the jury knew, the spring and summer were the harvest time of a painter and decorator, and during the whole of this time the plaintiff had been unable to earn anything at all. The doctor's bill amounted to £5, and the plaintiff was still suffering much pain from his injuries. After hearing the evidence, he (Mr. Burton) should ask the jury to find a verdict for the plaintiff, with such damages as they might think fair and reasonable.—He celled the plaintiff, who gave evidence of a confirmatory character. He had never previously worked on a scaffeld of that description. Some time after the accident he mot the defendant, and asked him . why he erected the scaffold of such inferior timber. The defendant replied that they must have all been of a "rook." Plaintiff said this was all nonsense, seeing that he fell on the floor at one corner, two men on the pulpit and the other two did ' not fall. Sines the accident be had male several attempts to resume his labeur, but had only done half a week's work. He had pains in his head, neck, and spine, and could not ascend a ladder without becoming dizzy. He reckoned his profits at £4 per week, viz., £2 10s. ' for his awn personal labour, 10s. for each man, and £1 each for the apprentices.—By Mr. Fletcher : He had no expe- rience of scaffolding. When they commenced work Heyes seemed frightened, and witness shook the scaffolding to set his doubts at rest, as he had confidence Mr. Statham would build it strong enough. Heyes shouted out that that was not the way to try the scaffolding. Middleton also coin- plained of the strength of the scaffold, but witness replied that it seamed "right enough."—Wm Middleton, painter, living, in Ellesmere-street, who fell with the scaffolding, ; described how the erection was made. Scantlings two inches by three and three inches by four, he stated, were used in- stead of scaffolding poles, and in the centre planks rested upon wood of this description. When he first saw it, he said to Mr. Frodsham and the men that those who erected it wanted six months, as it was not fit foe anybody to go on. Himself and the other painters then staved the erection with further pieces of scantling.—By Mr. Fletcher : The upright which broke would be about three cr four inches wide at the bottom, about 2A- at the top, and an inch thick. It was the edge of an inch board.—John byes, painter, 9, Union-street, Runcorn, said the scaffold was con- struc'ed of spruce spars, and he remarked at the time that they would break like carrots when four men got to work on them. The scaffold was not fit for four men to work upon. Mr. Statham Was present when he made these observations and said it was safe enough, for he and a labourer had been round it. After the accident he saw Mr. Statham, who said the scaffold would have done with another bearer or two at the pulpit end. He told witness to go home and "keep it quiet." The following day after the erection had been strengthened the men went on with the whitening.—Dr. McDoagell said in the forenoon of the 27th April he examined the plaintiff and found him in a dazed condition, recovering from concussion of the brain, and talk- ing incoherently. His head was bruised and the spine of the back was injured. On the following day there were feverish symptoms, and the plaintiff was threatened with brain issue. He had been under his care ever since, and was now. He was not fit for work, and further mischief might take place. He had known softening of the brain fol- low concussion of the brain after the lapse of six months. Cross-examined by Mr. Fletcher: He (witness) told Mr. Statham that the scaffolding was exceedingly weak for men to go upon.—Mr. Farrell, having great experience as a builder, described the scaffolding, which he did not consider was constructed of proper wood, but was safe everywhere but at the point where it fell. By Mr. Fletcher: He did not see the piece over the pulpit before it fell.—James Wilson, builder and contractor, Greenwav-roal, Runcorn, who flaW the scaffolding the day before the accident, was of opinion that it was not sufficiently strong, and he would not have worked upon it himself. By Mr. Fletcher: A prudent man would not have ventured upon it.—Michael Barker, surveyor to the Board of Commissioners, said he saw the scaffold after the accident. The piece that had broken was a "roofing spar." He was not in the place more than three minutes, and to him the scaffold seemed a slight thing, and he would not hive worked upon it himself.— Fur the defence, Mr. Fletcher stated that the plaintiff sas a man who by the -virtue of his occupation ought to have technical knowledge of what would be sufficient for the workmen he engaged. That day he said he had no special knowledge of scaffo'ding, but foitunately for him his lack of knowledge was on this occasion supplied by Hayes and Middleton, both of whom condemned the scaffolding, and told Frodsham that they were not satisfied with it. It was, therefore, an act of imprudence on their part to go upon it; they had no right there, and having done so it was at their own risk, and they were not entitled to recover from Mr. Statham, because there was what was known in law as con- tributory negligence. Mr. Fletcher pointed out that the witnesses for the plaintiff agreed in stating that corners of the platform were not disturbed at all; how then did the plaintiff fail? He ventured to submit that the staging upon which Frodsham stood did not give way at all, but that Frodsham, seeing the centre portion give way, became alarmed for his own safety and jumped down and received his injuries. If that was so, the defendant was not respon- sible for the accident, which was in no way attributable to him. On the other hand, if they thought Mr. Statham to

blame, he left the question of damages entirely in their hands.—His Honour then directed the jury at great 'length. observing that he did not agree with Mr. Fletcher that in attempting to strengthen the scaffolding the plaintiff and his men took the defects out of the hands of Statham —Thn. jury retired to consider their verdict, and after an absence of nearly an hour returned into court with a verdict for the plaintiff for £3O.
THE LATE MR. BILLINGSLEY, OF RUNCORN.

On Wednesday there was placed in the Primitive Metho- diet Chapel, Greenway-road, Runcorn, a marble tablet bear- ing the following inscription :—" In loving memory of - Elijah Billingsley, the first organist of this chapel, who died December 22nd, 1882, aged 31 years, this tablet was erected_ by his many friends as a mark of the great esteem and affec- tion they feel for him ass tribute to the fidelity and earnest- ness with which he laboured for the prosperity of the society; and as a sorrowful memento of his premature death. 'ln the midst of life we are in death.'" 'rhe tablet, which is of statuary marble, has been exfxuted with great taste by Mr. William Mossford, of Crewe. Mr. Billingsley, to whose memory the tablet is erected, was the compiler of a service of song entitled "The Basket of Flowers," and the tablet is surmounted by a representation of a basket of flowers; while at the foot of the inscription is a scroll of music, containing the opening lines of " The Orphan's Prayer," a piece which the deceased gentleman, composed specially for his service.

DISTRICT NEWS. , (Continued from page 6) AUTON GRANGE. STATE or THE CROPS —A correspondent at Acton Grange sends us the following report on the state of the crops:— " Hay : I consider to be about 30 per cent, less than an average crop, but I think most of it will be well secured. Potatoes: I think we shall have a good crop, as I never saw them looking better. Turnips are not looking quite as well as they ought to do at this season of the year, but they may yet come out a fair crop if we have a warm September and October. Second crops of potatoes and turnips, also clover, are looking only very middling' particularly clover, which must be very light. Beans: Not many grown about here. Oats and Wheat will, I think, cut up thin on the ground, though we cannot tell until we commence cutting, as they are very badly down with the heavy rains and wind lately. Wheat will be very late this season. ASTON GRANGE. THE CHARGE AGAINST A FARDItR'S SON.—Before the Rev. E. A. P. Campbell and Captain Hazlehurst, at Run- corn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Joseph Wilkinson, son of a farmer, was summoned on a charge of trespassing in search of game on land at Aston Grange, in the occupation of Col. Talbot, on the 22nd June.—Mr. Husband appeared for the prosecution, and Mr. W. H Linaker for the defendant.— The case was adjourned a month ago for the production of the deed of right to shoot over the ground.—After a short argument this was put in, and Mr. Linaker then required it to be proved.—Mr. Husband contended that this was un- necessary, but the magistrates ruled against him. Mr. Husband pointed out that the witnesses to the deed were solicitors in London, and that the expense of their atten- dance at court would be great; but Mr. Linaker said that was a question that did not arise at present, and, on the ground that the prosecutors had had five weeks to prove their case, asked that the defendant should be dismiseed.— Mr. Campbell said as the objection was a technical one they adjourned the case a month.—Mr. Linaker then ap- plied for the costs of the day, but the Bench declined to make the order.

div.p: DI TTON.

ASSAULT ON THE POLICE AT DITTON.-At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, a young man named Henry Atkin- son was charged with being drunk and disorderly, with 51- saulting P. 0., Bruce, and injuring his uniform to the extent of is. At midnight on Friday the defendant, who was drunk, was creating a disturb,ince in Hale-road, Ditton. He challenged a Man to fight, and P.C. Bruce requested him to go home. He then abused the officer, striking him on the forehead with some bard implement, and tore his coat. The officer was compelled to use his staff, and succeeding in put- ting the handcuffs on, with great difficulty got him to the police station.—For .the assault the defendant was fined lOs and costs lie 6d ; for being drunk 5s and costs, and a similar penalty for the damage to the coat ; or in default 2 days' hard labour.

div.p: FRODSHAM.

TRINITY WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS' TRIP.— rue teachers at the Trinity Wesleyan Sunday School and their friends to the number of 29 went to Bettws-y-coed on Monday, when, notwithstanding the unfavourable weather, a pleasant day was,spent, and the Swallow Waterfalls, Fairy Glen, and other places of interest at this popular resort will long be remembered by the visitors. ACCIDENT IN CHURCH-STREET.—An accident occurred in Church-street, Frodshasa, on Saturday, to Joseph Dunbeb- bin, coachman to Mr. John Simpson, of Dunsdale, caused by the spirited horse which he was riding stumbling near the Liverpool House, throwing him against the curbstones and seriously injuring his back. The injured man was taken borne in a carriage, and is recovering from the accident.

ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT FRODSHAM BRIDGE.-011 Sun- day considerable excitement was caused by a report that a man named Clifford Hoskin had made a desperate attempt to commit suicide. It appeared that Hoskin and his wife had been living with John Greenway, at Frodsharn Bridge, for about four months, and in a fit of passion on Sunday morn- ing he seized a razor and inflicted serious injury on his throat and left arm. The wound in the thrcat was stitched up by Dr. Shaw, and Mr. Riley, the relieving officer, had the man promptly conveyed to the Workhuse Hospital at Dutton, where he is progressing favourably towards re- covery.

HALEWOOD PARISH CHURCIL—The dedication SerViCU; in connection with the new tower and octave of bells were continued on Sunday last, when special and appropriate ser— mons were preached; in the rsotning by the rector, the Rev. T. Chamber., M.A., and in the afternoon by the Rev. J. W. Diggle, M.A., of Mossley Hill. The collections in aid of parochial accounts amounted in the aggregate to the handsome total of £6B is 11d. HOLLINS GREEN.

A WIFE LOST.—Frank Petford, Red Lion Inn, Hollins Green was summoned at Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday, for assaulting Nathaniel Carter, of Manches- ter, on the 30th ult. There wts a cross-summons in which Petford charged Carter with assault.—Mr. Garth- waite, Manchester, appeared for Petford.—Carter, who throughout the proceedings appeared very excited, said that on the afternoon of the day named, he came, as he had often done before, from Manchester to the Red Lion, Hollins Green. He spent a good deal of time helping to make hay, and in the evening he was standing with his back to a machine talkinre to Petford, when the latter, without any provocation, called him a sot, gave him a blow knocking him on to the machine. and then went into him with his feet, and in an instant he was pouring with blood. There was no one in the field at the time. and Petford before strik- ing him appeared to be very friendly. He (complainant) eauld show twenty letters from Petford to show " My dear Sf- I vu an ttsv luttn luaLlvu I can respecting your wife."—lt was elicited during cross- examination that Carter's wife had left him, and that he did not know where she was, but he was under the impres- sion her whereabouts was known at the Red Lion.—P.C. 302 said that Carter came to his station on the night in question, and complained that he had been badly used. He was bleeding from the mouth at the time. He was not sober. —Frank Petford said that when the row commenced Carter said to him "Come here, I have a crow to pick with you." He then asked complainant where his wife was, but witness told him he did not know, whereupon Carter struck witness twice with his umbrella, and a struggle ensued.—Mrs. Pet- ford, landlady of the Red Lion, said that Carter often came to her house, and was constantly making enquiries about his wife. She had frequently asked him to leave the premises, and she had done so several times on the day in question. Carter's wife had been at her house, but not since she separ- ated from her husband.—The case against Petford was dismissed, and Carter was bound over in his own recognis- ances.

REFUSING TO QUIT. —Thomas Hinton, labourer, of Lymtn, was summoned at Lyinm Petty Sessions, yesterday, for being drunk on licensed premises and refusing to quit.—P.C. 115 said that on the 28th ult. he WAS at Booth's Hill, and heard a disturbance in the Crown Inn. He went inside and found defendant using very had language, and refusing to quit. Mrs. Nagle asked him to put the defendant out, and he did so.—A fine of 5s and costs was imposed. THE RUSH-BEARING.—This festival, though it attracted a good number of persons to the village, passed off very quietly, even more so than in former years. There was almost an entire absence of that dissipation and rowdyism which characteris s similar festivals, and the police bad not a single case of drunkenness to report. As we noticed last week, the Local B ,ard had issued notices prohibiting erec- tions in the streets or near the Cross, and the inevitable nserry-go-rounds, swings, hobby-horses, Arc., were deposited in a field to the rear of the police station, where the itinerants catered for the patronage of tire juveuiles and the young men and maidens who paid them a visit. The villagers are very jealous as to their ancient rights and customs, and the action of the Board seems to have given rise to considerable dissatisfaction. It is thought by many that their rights have been arbitrarily dealt with by the Board, but they have submitted to the change without any public demonstration of feeling. One man, however, has been more bold than the rest for on Tues- day afternoon he threw down the gauntlet to the Board by erecting a stall near the Cross, but no action has been taken against him so far. About 1,300 persons left the town for Blackpool by the trip which had been organised by Wesievan, Independent, Congregational, and Primitive Methodist bodies, and there was no casualty of any moment.

Tun THEFT orA COAT.— Uhomas Burke, a young man, a resident of Moore, was charged, on remand, at Warring- ton Police Court, on "Monday, with stealing, on or about the 3rd January last, a uniform topcoat, value £l, from a van in Arpley Station goods yard, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Co.—The erkence, which was reported in The Examiner of last week, was again repeated. —Prisoner, in answer to the charge, pleaded not guilty, and stated that he found the coat at Slutebors-lane crossing.— The Bench, however, were convinced of the prisoner's guilt, and ordered him to pay 20s. and costs, or go to prison for a month.

THE FATHER OF PRIMITIVE IVIHTHODISX.—On Tuesday night a most interesting gathering of Nonconformists from all parts of England assembled at Chorley, near Nantwich, when Mr. Thomas Bateman was presentc,; with portraits, in ail, of himself and wife, in recognition of his services as connexional auditor of the Primitive Methodist denomina- tion. Mr. Bateman, who was barn in 1799, is over 34 years of age. He joined Primitive Methodism in 1819, and took an active part in introducing Methodism into Cheshire, Lan- cashire, and the Potteries. Mr. Bateman for many years regularly took alternate services in Manchester, Liverpool, Chester, the Potteries, and Shrewsbury, frequently walking twenty miles to take service at half-past ten at the Chester Cross. Mr. Bateman was elected a permanent member of the Primitive Methodist Conference, then connexional auditor, and twice he has been president of the Conference. Mr. James Toinkinsan, Will ington Hall, 1 arporley, made the presentation on behalf of the officers and leading members of the Conference and the general denomination. SANDBACH.

FEVER AT SANDBACIL—Fever has broken out in several streets in Sandbach, and a strong complaint has been sent to the Local Government Board, charging. the Sandbach Local Board with making default in dealing with drainage and not obtaining a proper water supply. The sources from whence the township draws its water have been analysed by the Local Government Board's chemist, who condemns ten out of the twelve samples as little better than sewage rater. The remaining two samples are not tecornmended,

Sir,—Dr. McDougall's letter in your issue of the 4;b inst., supplements his speech at the last Commissioners' meeting. He is afraid it was not made clear at that meeting that the observation-of a member at the meeting of June 27th, 1881, had reference to professional feeling, and was not an attempt to force the hand of the Law Clerk, as the doctor's traducers would nave the ratepayers to believe. The doctor's letter does not throw much light upon the subject. Perhaps he will enlighten your readers by explaining what this profes- sional feeling is to which he refers. Ido not see it clear at all how the observations of the member had refer- ence to professional feelings, and await the expla- nation. It is evident that the doctor does not fully understand the meaning of some werds he uses when in a temp3r. Traducer 13 a long word for him to use, and he either dues not know its true meaning or he does not remember what really took place on the Ist inst. I will briefly mention the facts which came out at that meeting as reported in your columns of August 4th, show- ing his responsibility, and, as now appears, that of Mr. W. Handiey, in the institution of the law psoceedings, which the doctor wishes the public to believe he had nothing par- ticular to do with. Firstly, it was stated that, under the strong advice and recommendation of Dr. McDougall, the resolution to take proceedings against Mr. Beasley was passed. The doctor does not deny this statement. Secondly, that it was at the instance of the doctor and his friend Mr. Handley that the committee was called to- gether. The secretary conveniently forgets how the calling of the meeting originated, but he was reminded of it by Mr. Norman, who was chairman of that meeting, and who says he complained to the Secretary that the meeting had been called without his permission, and Mr. Brookes answered that Dr. McDougall said it was an important thing, and he must call the meeting at once. To confirm which Mr. Norman referred to Mr. Speakman, or any other member, if tie did or did not question the Secretary about it, and ask him who authorised the meeting, to which Mr: Speakman replied, "That is so." Lastly, that the doctor and Mr. Handley advised and urged the course to be taken, and on the Law Clerk raising an objection, he was told that if he refused to act some other lawyer would be got to do it. Mr. Linaker says that he hesitated as to accepting instruc- tions, and one of the committee stated that evidently he ob- jected to act upon the instructions, and it was also sup;- gested that the Commissioners give instructions to some one else to act in the matter. Therefore, as every statement made at the meeting was proved, the doctor must have still been in a fog when he wrote the letter to the Guardian. Passing over his exalted utterances, we come to the rehearsal between himself and the Law Clerk of a few items of the bill of costs. This the doctor said was very painful to him, but none of us could _

understand how a true statement of items from a document should be a painful operation to him, and as none of the Commissioners had seen the bill but himself, we could not see through this painful business until Messrs. Jones and Pride's letter appeared, which says, "The further observa- tions to counsel composing the other items in the bill, of which Dr. McDougall made so much, had nothing whatever to do with any statements made by Mr. Speakman or Dr. Steele." This being the case, and tilt, painful business shown in its true light, surely the Doctor will make an ample apology to the gentleman he so grossly misrepre- sented. ROST. SHAW.

div.head: OUR NATIONAL CHURCH.
div.p: OUR NATIONAL CHURCH.

Sir,—By your kind permission, I would like to say a few words in answer to some of the remarks made by Mr. H. J. Westbrook, on a letter written by " Clifford Dix," which appeared in The Examinei• of Saturday, July 28th. lam a little disappointed that " Clifford Dix " has not answered young Churchman's letter, though I was pleased to see one of " Clifford Dix's" statements confirmed in your issue a Saturday last hp t‘ Viaitnr " fin re(nronen en Trinity Church), and I have no doubt that most, if not all, the other statements made by "Clifford Dix" can be confirmed. In the first place, he begins with Orange Lodges, Church Defence Associations; c tring nothiag for the glory of God or the salvation of His people. And is it not true ? Would it not be more suitable to call them the picnic and pleasure associations, for I believe those things occupy some of their thoughts far more than does the welfare of their fellow men. Then H. J. W. brings Bradlaugh forward. Now, sir, lam afraid "Clifford Dix" must have tread on Young Churchman's toes, or why should he introduce such a question in a subject of this sort. The next thing he touches upon is Dissenters and Disestablishment ; one of thp main argumetts of the Dissenters being that the parsons look too much after the loaves and fishes and neglect their flock, which statement I can personally say is true. Perhaps Yowl.. Churchman (for he himself says be is young) resides under the parental roof. If so, rates do not trouble him; but I am sorry to say they do me, in par- ticular the rates for the support of this national Church. I have lived here over one half dezen years, and never, but once, has a Church of England clergyman called on me to ask if I had either soul or body, but the rates are collected. regular enough (so what about the loaves and fishes). Un- fortunately I am a workingman, and cannot send an invita- tion to our parson asking him to attend a lawn tennis match or drawing-room party, or doubtless I should receive far more of his clerical services; neither am I a solitary in- stance, for there are many who help to pay the piper, but never get any of his music. What about empty pleas? Are the Church of England gentry so poor that we Dissenters must help to keep their parsons? I fancy "Young Chu-ch- man " might analyse (with no satisfaction to himself if truly done) some of the Dissenting sect with the clergy of his own Church. I knew one a short distance from here that would not have objected to short prayers if the bounds happened to meet near by, and would stand and see the fox torn to pieces though in half an hour after I woull not like to have been one of his scholars, caught by him, setting a terrier at a cat up a tree. One is cruelty, what is the other? Young Churchman may say this is ignorance, but are there not scores of fox-hunting parsons who think quite as much of a fox as they do of the souls in their parish, and yet I fancy I can see the look of scorn that would cross Young Church- man's righteous countenance, did he happen to see a Dissen- ting parson after the hounds. If we touch the question of hire, I should say that on the average the Church of Eng- land clergy receive five times the amount of salary that Dis- senting ministers do; their hire is not paid by Church of Eng- land people, but by Dissenters only. It appears to me that Young Churchman's acquaintance with good church clergy- men is very limited, as he only speaks of one as ',worthy of his hire (the vicar of Holy Trinity). Though I am a Dis- senter I am pleased to say I have known two whose daily life and actions proved them to be Christians, and to whom I believe their hire was as nothing; but duty towards God and man is everything to them. New, sir, with another rem irk or two I will close my epistle, which is longer than I intended it to be. About the misrepresentation of the church; is there no cause for it? Cause and effect generally go together, and I think to all unbiased mind' the cease is very apparent. One remark is in reference to Joseph Arch and his statement at New- castle; that might not be true But what about the case in Cheshire here, that went the round of the papers a short time since? Was that untrue? And again, in reference to the auTiences; did Mr. H. J. W. ever see an audience of 100 people in which there was not some few ordinary intelligent ones? I believe it would be almost impossible to get to- gether an audience of people without some common-sensible followers amongst them, and some, I should think, whose intelligence was superior to Mr. H. J. W.'s, whose sense appears to be very common indeed in that which is right and honest.—! am, sir, yours, A DISSENTER. Frodsham, August 16th. rawerff..ll,4l/NMIMMO

LAWN TENNIS: LANCASHIRE V. CHESEIEE.—This tour- nament for a challenge shield was continued on Saturday, at tM ground of the Northern Lawn Tennis Association, Old Trafford, by representatives of clubs hailing from the above shires. The ground was very heavy from recent rains. The semi-final and final were, however, got through in spite of the unpropitous state of the weather, and at the close Hooton was declared the winners. Details of play—Semi- float : Mr. Richardson (ffieton) beat Mr. H. R. Slielmerdine (Vagrants) by 2 sets to love, 6-0, 6-1 ; Mr:F. W. J( nes (Hooton) beat Mr. P. W. Allen (Vagrants) by 2 sets to love, 6-2, 6 ; Mr. R. Jones (Hooton) beat Mr. J. E. Flete•er (Vagrants) by 2 sets to 1, 5-6, 6-5, 6-4; Mr. A. P. Jones beat Mr. H. F. Hufore by 2 sets to 1,4-6, 6 0, 6 4; Hooton 4 matches to love. Bowden v. Waterloo : Mr. R. J. Kerr (Bowdon) beat Mr. A. G. Rae (Waterloo) by 2 sets to love, 6-5, 6-3 ; Mr. A. THE ALLEGED ILLEGAL REMOVAL OF GOODS.—At Run- corn Petty Sessions, on Monday, the adjourned summons against Thomas Nolan, of Weston, for having, on the 19th July, clandestinely and frandulentl`Y removed goods and chattels of the value of £2 to some place unknown, in order to prevent the landlord, John Houghton, of Runcorn, dis- training for arrears of rent, was heard.—Mr. Burton ap- peared for the defendant.—The evidence for the prosecution has been published.—For the defence Mr. Burton stated that on the 19th July the defendant owed the complainant £1 15s. for rent, and the latter on that day removed every- thingfrom the house vr bile the defendant was at his work. The door of the house was locked and the defendant's wife and children were without shelter, but a neighbour kindly gave them protection. The articles alleged to have been clandestinely removed were sold to a neighbour in May in order that the defendant's wife might visit her sick mother in Ireland. There was no evidence of clandestine remoVal. —Catherine Richt ey and Mrs. Welch havint been examined, the Bench dismissed the case.

TRESPASSING IN PURSUIT OF GAR R AT WINWICK.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, William Mains (who did not appear), was summoned for trespassing in pursuit of game on land at Winwick, in the occupatian of Mr. Hopwood and Mr. Stone, on the Ist July. Mr. Moore appeared for the complainants. About half-oast five on the morning of the date named two keepers were watching the land in question when they saw the defendant spread two nets over some rabbit burrows. The defendant had a rabbit in his possession, and on seeing the keepers he ran away, and secreted himself in a wood.—Fined 40s and costs, or, in default of payment, one month's imprisonment.

THE CHESHIRE DAIRY FARMERS' A SSOCIATION.—Thi association, which was established under the presidency of the Duke of Westminster to encourage the production and distribution of Cheshire theese, has decided to hold its annual exhibition at Chester on the 16th and 17th of Oc- tober. There are ten classes, in which handsome prizes are given, all of which are open to the shirs and all parts of Lancashire, Derbyshire, Staffordshire, Shropshire, and Flintshiro within ten miles of the border. POACHING AFFRAY.—A serious poaching affray occurred early on Tuesday morning at Capesthorne, Cheshire, the seat of Mr. Bromley-Divenport, M.P., when ten poachers attacked three keepers with stones and bludgeons. In the encounter two of the poachers were felled by the keepers, and the remainder made off, leaving a quantity of nets behind them. The two captured men, Peter Bayley and Samuel Higgin, both of Romiley, were brought before the magistrates at Macclesfield, and fined £5 each.

ATTEMPTED CHILD 'MURDER A/CD SUICIDE. Robert Jones, foreman at a wine and spirit vaults, is in the cus- tody of the Chester police, charged with attempting to murder his child and commit suicide. It is said that he first dashed ti)e child's head against a telegraph pole and then threw it into the canal, into which he himself after- wards jumped. Apparently sobered by the cold water, he subsequently seized the child and handed it to its mother. and then was himself dragged out of the canal. Before the magistrates he denied all intention of killing the child.

ATTACKING A CHESHIRE DOCTOR ON THE HIGHWAY.— On Tuesday, at Broxton, two rongh-looking fellows named Burke and Clevin, were committed to Chester assizes for assaulting Dr. Proudlove, Tattenhall, and demanding money, with violence. The prisoners came up to Dr. Proud- love as he was driving on the highway near Broxton, and when he refused to buy a comb one prisoner seized the horses' head while the other gripped Dr. Proudlove's arm with great violence. In order tr, escape from them Dr. Proudlove gave them sixpence. The prisoners were after- wards arrested hy the Cheshire police, when pedlars' licenses and 23. were found upon them.

CIIFSTER AND TIM ROYAL AGRICULTURAL Sow.—On Vonday afternoon the Mayor of Chester converted a meet- ing at the Town Hall, with the object of taking initiatory steps towards inviting the Council of the Royal Agricul- tural Society to hold its meeting at Chester in 1885. The Han. C. Parker, a member of the Council, said he thought if proper steps were adopted the Council might be disposed to bring the show to Chester. A telegram was read from the Duke of Westminster expressing regret that he was unable to attend, and sympathising with the object of the meeting. Mr. H. E. Taylor said that the Royal Show, according to the rule, must in 1885 be held in Lancashire, Cheshire, or North Wales. He thought it would be unfair if the show were again taken into Lancaahire, where it had been held very frequently. The Town Clerk said the Society wenAd require subscriptions amounting to £3,000, but that sum, he thought, would readily be subscribed. The Rhoodee would be- most admirably adapted for the show. (Hear, hear.) A committee was then formed and a formal resolution adopted that the Royal Agricultural Society should be invitsd to hold its show at Chester in 1885.
